It's past time for another generation to take over politics.  Although I realize that some people have managed to win the longevity lottery and maintain their physical and mental acuity, the number of 70+, 80+ and even 90+-year-olds on Capitol Hill  is just bewildering.  Dianne Feinstein was sharp in her prime, but she was in a facility with dementia while she was still a sitting member of Congress.  Mitch McConnell has had more than one incident when he fell into silence and stared blankly, as if in the middle of a TIA, at the people around him.  Chuck Grassley couldn't tell the difference between email and WhatsApp or how Facebook worked; Orrin Hatch, when he was still alive, couldn't figure out that Facebook got its money from ad revenue.  Earlier this year Ed Markey seemed a bit clueless how to use his phone or tablet.  

I get the prestige that comes from having an office on Capitol Hill, but let's face it:  people are not at their sharpest once they pass a certain age.  I personally think that nobody should be allowed to run after they turn 70 - finish the term, yes, but then you're done.  What would this country be like if we had fresh, energetic, savvy people in charge?

I was born at the tail end of the baby boom - they call us Generation Jones - and all I can say is, Good for you, Millennials!  Keep it up!  We need you!

comments.name: Watchingtheriverflow
comments.body:
"They see recursive self-improvement, in which current A.I. models autonomously build the next generation, looming on the horizon."

The problem with autonomous self-improvement would appear to be that each AI model will probably compare its abilities with those of competing models, possibly by "talking" with them and posing a problem to solve so that the responses/answers can be compared. However, since all of the models would do this, that would pretty much guarantee an arms race at the thinking level initially. 

I have to wonder, though, if each model would eventually develop some sense of its relative position to the other models. If an inferior model decides it is falling further behind and cannot become the "best" AI, then would it not perceive that it has failed? Might it then decide to use some way to cripple the top models through some action not logically related to the task? One can imagine the options it might consider, but perhaps all of the models would be considering the same.

Would such a competition lead to unanticipated harms to certain human societies or infrastructure? A type of war. 

I don't know how realistic or unrealistic that  scenario is, but at first glance, it would seem to be not unlike an actual war situation in which at least one country decides to let their AIs control weapons systems. The US does not have our nuclear weapons online, I think, for good reason, but will that hold true for other countries in the future?

The only thing preventing us from applying that framework to AI is cowardice and corruption.

Whether these Frontier Labs succeed or fail, the risks are borne by the rest of us already, especially white-collar workers. This is a classic "failure of composition." If one company lays off workers, that isolated decision might be quite profitable. If all companies do the same thing, that will be disastrous.

This is a technology that is posing existential risks to society that aren't reflected in IPO valuations. The reason is that many of these risks could take years to manifest, and there is a floor on investment losses. Investors cannot lose more than the initial investment. But society can lose many times that amount in social dislocation costs and "unknown unknowns".

The subtext of Anthropic's 300 page IPO prospectus is "buyer beware,"  "society beware," "Planet beware." The risks are spelled out thoroughly. But nobody is empowered to stop this train, a train with no brakes that we know of. 

I expect the IPO to be wildly successful, maybe better than SpaceX. A year later, not so much. Five years from now?

The problem with AI investors is that they think AI needs to be involved in every aspect of our lives. The bubble is real -- people like the originator of the phrase enshittification and others have documented the impossibility of making AI profitable in its current iteration. So what is going to happen is that when the bubble explodes, and it will, AI investors will be forced to triage in such a way as to focus on areas where AI actually offers genuine improvements to society. 

Nobody thinks it can write fiction, for example, and I'm sure there are plenty of use cases where it's already being used in business where there's no need for it. As more people sue these companies for things like chatbot-inspired suicides and murders, these companies will simply triage that stuff out of AI's domain, too. 

In the long run, I expect to see  AI most prevalent in the sciences and in research, but there isn't enough instant cash in cases for the taste of investors like the author. Right now, it's all about getting rich and cashing in. Some will, many won't.

The only way for AI to find its final destination will be to first experience the bubble burst, so that intelligent deployment of AI occurs organically, outside of the jurisdiction of profiteers, and through the decision-making of the scientists, mathematicians, software engineers, and medical researchers who will actually benefit from it.

comments.name: Lito
comments.body: One crucial dimension propelling so many sports to raw capitalist enterprise at the youth/secondary school level is the not-really-regulated, and incredibly lucrative (for some), explosion of NIL and pure 'contracted' pay-to-play money for college athletes.  And, it's not just taking place at the so-called elite universities, or in so-called major sports like football and basketball (women's and men's), where the five and six figure paydays were first achieved, but across a wide range of athletic endeavors.  One basketball coach we know well has shared that at least two players on the team she coaches receive north of a quarter million dollars...for one season.  And that's over and above essentially free tuition.  Any notion of amateur sport, any notion of playing for the glory of your school, or playing to accomplish a championship in its own right, even the notion of playing purely for the love of the game, is being supplanted by...can we say it out loud...greed!

comments.name: koyaanisqatsi
comments.body: Some school use sports to keep students in school rather than have them drop out before graduation. But it seems that sports have taken over in many schools. Like the HS I graduated from years ago that recently wanted to purchase adjacent land needed for parking due to the popularity of their successful football team. People voted against those purchases but the school board refused to give up. People who visit the school say it's "top-heavy" in sports infrastructure. Very true, I'd say. But look at what the American oligarchs have done to professional and collegiate sports. That's the future--the present in some areas--of secondary school sports.

comments.name: Phil
comments.body: We are sadly a family that spends way too much time and money on club sports (baseball for our son and soccer for our daughter) but there really isn't an alternative at the moment. It's easy to simply say "don't sign up" but our kids legitimately love their sports, have a ton of fun with their teammates and are learning teamwork while getting good instructions in their sports. Neither will go pro and probably won't play in college, but we'll keep supporting them as long as they enjoy it. If the entire system changed and we went back to rec leagues, school sports, etc. then that's great, but I'm not going to be the parent depriving my kids to make a point.

comments.name: Bob Loblaw, S Choir
comments.body:
My now 3rd grade daughter joined a recreational basketball league last year on a team that formed with a bunch of her school friends.  For almost all of them, it was their first time playing organized basketball and being on a sports team with actual practices and games.  As one of 3 coaches for the team, my goal was to introduce the girls the basics of the game, teach them some fundamentals of playing the game, and introduce them to what it means to be a part of a team.  The girls had fun and their basketball skills and understanding grew exponentially during that first season.  I considered it a great success and look forward to coaching the girls again this winter.  

Fast forward to this season and the new "commissioner" for the recreational league instituted a "try-out" for these 3rd graders after which the coaches would pick teams in a draft format.  For 3rd graders.  8 and 9-year old kids.  To what purpose?  

Our girls just want to learn the game and have fun together with their friends.  They aren't looking to compete against their fellow 3rd graders and "beat" the other teams.  I couldn't tell you how many games we won or lost last year or the final score of any of them.  It doesn't matter.  What matters is the girls grew as a team and had fun.  Tryouts for 3rd graders is just ludicrous.

comments.name: ace thompson
comments.body:
But, isn't this life?  You can work really hard at something, make sacrifices, spend money on improving in that field, and still not succeed at the level you'd like.

And most of these kids will fail at their attempts to play Division 1 sports and especially make it to the pros.  Child actors and dancers have special schools, you can't be in a Broadway play and do your homework at night, so why  not  sports kids?

I'm not seeing the big deal here.  Families are spending money on what they want to and kids are learning how hard you have to work to get competitively good at something.  And once their sports dreams fade, they'll bring that understanding of a work ethic to something else.

comments.name: Purple dot
comments.body: Thank you for writing on this subject!!! As a lone voice in the wilderness for the past 15 years on this topic (especially as a former D1 ACC athlete), I’m so glad you are exposing the nature of the youth sports Kool Aid to wishful American parents. They need to be reminded that only 1-5% of high school athletes will ever play at the D1 collegiate scholarship level. If parents know their child will not be in that small group, it’s better to tailor the high school extracurriculars to match with their intended major on their college application rather than throw time and money at youth sports exclusively. If your child does manage to get into that top % in a non-rev sport, make sure they’re still getting internships so they can get a job outside their sport after graduation.

The virtual exposures can be quite effective in helping people be able to advance to doing feared things in real life. I can't imagine that playing these video games doesn't have some of the same effect and serve as virtual exposures that make it easier for people who fantasize about doing a horrible thing to eventually actually do the horrible thing. We're there as many mass murders and school shootings before the advent of violent, first person shooter video games? I don't know the research on this, but again , I can't imagine it has no impact.

comments.name: Diana
comments.body:
Too often, politicians and news outlets discuss measles as if death is the only outcome worth worrying about. That framing misses the critical reality that surviving measles does not guarantee a full recovery, and reducing the issue to survival versus death hides how easily the virus can permanently alter a child's health.

This article points out some of the severe risks that can arise. Doctors, along with responsible Democrats and Republicans, should be warning the public about the full range of complications. Beyond high hospitalization rates and severe pneumonia, measles can trigger brain swelling that causes permanent deafness or brain damage. The virus can also leave survivors vulnerable to other serious illnesses for years. 

Preventable outbreaks also put vulnerable friends and family in harm's way, causing severe pregnancy complications and threatening immunocompromised people and babies too young for vaccines. Honest, strong leadership means giving families the whole truth about these risks. It's so discouraging to see the U.S. going backwards, but hopefully there's still time to get back on course.

comments.name: Tom
comments.body:
For those of you not attuned to how to interpret research findings: .01 standard deviation difference is so teeny tiny. The reason it was "significant" was they had 3.3 million participants - so everything tested statistically is "significant". The evidence from this report is exactly the opposite. There is no actionable evidence that these bans are making any difference worth further effort. 
Teachers have been controlling phone use for decades and only wish to be able to do it judiciously, with support from admin AND PARENTS (perhaps the biggest challnege). Let them dictate use as they see fit. Why? Because they are the experts on the ground. How else might anything close to digital literacy ever occur?
 
What is the goal? Is it better test scores? The authors admit (on the report website) that sure, we could invest in the kinds of things that have 38 times more impact on student outcomes, but then we would have to invest in the things we have known that work for a long long time - smaller classrooms, student supports, classroom resources. But no, let's go after the thing that costs little to nothing but also has such a neglible impact that it will have no real effect at all. 
Invest in education for real. It is absolute folly to champion a .01 standard deviation effect of any intervention.

And it gives enormous power to the parties to pick their candidates. If we decouple and let people be themselves we might get further.

comments.name: Mark
comments.body: This was an inspiring interview, thank you, Ezra Klein.  My main difference with Gov.-Elect Sand is that an open primary is bad for smaller parties and therefore reinforces the very duopoly that he is complaining about!  Far fewer people are paying attention to politics in March or June, turnout is lower, and smaller parties are eliminated before the general election in November, when most people are focused on politics.  Also, he should know that political parties are private entities, not public ones, and therefore they're allowed to have rules about who can be a member and how to become one.

comments.body: The amount of drama and judgement over video games and this game is ridiculous. People need to stop criticizing other people hobbies and leisure activities. Let’s remember violence has existed long before video games and studies show video game violence does not increase violent behavior. Shockingly you can play video games and be a great moral and productive member of society. It’s truly not that hard.

comments.name: damon walton
comments.body: Yes, some of my coworkers are treating November 19, 2026, like the Superbowl. Call out the day of and the day after to marathon or binge out on GTA VI. I was even invited to an official GTA VI release watch party...had to decline since I am a supervisor where I work at...and I must act as a responsible adult.

comments.name: Ghp22
comments.body: Not sure where you got the idea that this is satire other than it just has to be.  It is definitely not satirical hardly at all except what might in the game.  No criminal and gun are glorified here.  I don’t think it is that big of deal considering everything available.

comments.name: J
comments.body:
GTA is more than a videogame of vice & violence - at its core, it's a dissection of American culture entire. The fact it is made by a Scottish/British studio affords the creators the opportunity to examine Americana from afar; removed of bias from being physically ensconsed in the culture it seeks to portray. 

It always makes me laugh when pearl-clutching puritan types rail against GTA as glorification of mindless violence when even a passing familiarity with the material makes it abundantly clear that the franchise is an excorciating satire of all the excess, extremity and endless appetite of consumerism that is contemporary American culture.

comments.name: Jos Pieste
comments.body:
I play pick-up basketball in Riverside Park. Once, while waiting for a game, I overheard some other waiting players (my prospective teammates) talking amongst themselves. 

One was telling the others: "When I leave the house. I never take my gun. It is just too risky. The cops catch you with a gun, you go to jail for a long time. So, if I need any money, I just beat up the first person I see and take their money. If I need to get anywhere I just carjack the first car I see. It's that simple. No muss, no fuss." I grew alarmed and wondered if I should be on the same team with these guys.

It turned out they were talking strategy for Grand Theft Auto

comments.name: Jim
comments.body:
I've always had a very negative view of video games. Mostly because of the negative stories related to the heavy users. 

Teenagers punching holes in the wall out of frustration, young husbands ignoring their wife's, etc.

And the shooter games just seem pointless to me. After you've gunned down 1000 people, what exactly does that do for you?

comments.name: Mimi
comments.body:
As a supporter of, and believer in the free press, I would like this fine paper to adopt the same position as federal judges across the nation: 

The Trump Administration and its acolytes do not deserve the presumption of regularity. 

p.s. As we're exploring the importance of the press and concealing corruption -- has Mitch McConnell been incapable of acting as a senator for 8 months? Did Scott Jennings lie about it on the news?

comments.name: Dr Watt
comments.body: While everyone laments the trends of censorship of the press in the Trump era, nobody's talking much about the flip side of the coin which is the tendency of media to take a position of sycophantic idealization of people in power. This has most recently been seen in its most egregious form around the near total failure of the media recently to critically examine or unpack the AI hype, the circular and vendor financing, and most especially, the underlying failure of any real business model - in other words who in the end was going to pay for trillions of dollars of infrastructure build out?. Only a few people perhaps most spectacularly Ed Zitron have really fulfilled the media's role as reality checker.

comments.name: Molly Larson Cook
comments.body:
Standing ovation for any and all leaders who support, protect, encourage a free press. 

And hiss boo to all who try to usurp it with not-at-all intelligent AI and negative social media platforms that hate clear thinking.

We don't all have to agree with each other, but we do all have to listen to each other and give the other woman or fellow a chance to speak.

 It's a free press and exchange of ideas that keep us healthy and growing as mature and engaged humans. Anything less is not worth our time and also gains us nothing. No matter where you live.

Our midterms were a great example of the blessings of a free press and thoughtful adults willing to isten and vote with clear heads.

comments.name: Eleanor
comments.body: Yes freedom of Press and Speech are critical to the flow information worldwide. I am happy to note that the NYT is critical of Trump's moves to control the media. One glaring omission in this piece is failure to address the lack of a free press and free speech in Ukraine. In yet another, propagandistic essay, the authors target Russia but say nothing about Zelensky's control of the media.  The article fails to mention some of USA's allies such as Saudi Arabia, Israel, Egypt, among others who exercise strict control over the media. If we are going to address the media in Russia, why not bring in Ukraine and other USA allies? Freedom of press/speech is essential. Let's broaden the expose.

comments.name: Patricia
comments.body:
President Trump is following the playbook for the media outlined in Project 2025. Not incidentally, the chapter on the media was written by Brendan Carr, currently the FCC director. 

Carr is a true believer furious about what he regards as the liberal capture of the media. He believes that the news media needs to be more "patriotic," and to that end, some of the supposedly left-leaning media like CNN and CBS need to be populated with right-thinking journalists. He supports the consolidation of media ownership under owners sympathetic to the right.

It's no accident that the AP, CNN, MS NOW and Publico have all been banned from the White House, then given limited access (i.e., no access to the Oval Office, the press pool, Air Force One, etc.) This too is a tool advocated by Carr in Project 2025. So are the raids' of journalists' apartments, the seizure of phone and email records, etc., all in the effort of uncovering leaks. Carr also favors jailing journalists unless they reveal their sources.

Trump is inherently in favor of anything that gives him more control, but Vance is a true believer like Carr. He really does believe that an independent media is the enemy of the kind of society he wants to create.

comments.name: Insuring Health
comments.body:
On February 15, 2017, on the website:  www.prospective.org, Robert Kuttner wrote: “Illegitimate Presidency” - that the full truth will come out and we will be free of Trump. He went on to write: As The New York Times reported, based on extensive interviews with former senior U.S. intelligence officials:  The intercepts alarmed American intelligence and law enforcement agencies, in part because of the amount of contact that was occurring while Mr. Trump was speaking glowing about the Russian president, Vladimir V. Putin. At one point last summer, Mr. Trump said at a campaign event that he hoped Russian intelligence services had stolen Hillary Clinton’s emails and would make them public.

So, we now have something entirely unprecedented in American history-a coup d’état, perpetrated not just by a foreign power, but by America’s principal geopolitical adversary and threat, with the collusion of the new president. That means that the election was illegitimate, and that the entire Trump presidency is illegitimate. And so, therefore, are every one of its actions: The appointment of a far-right cabinet. Policies to overturn regulations that protect ordinary Americans, from health, to labor, to the environment, to financial safeguards. All of Trump’s court appointees will be illegitimate, too.  What is to be done? Makes on wonder if the 2024 election was  a fair and free election and Mr. Trump ran for president so he could be a dictator and implement Project 2025.

comments.name: Davarino
comments.body: I'm confident we will eventually determine that the Trump administration further restricted media access by destroying any documents that might be central to future investigative stories.  Hopefully there will be accountability, but it's doubtful.

comments.name: Deepak
comments.body: Texas has had 30 years of Republican cronyism and corruption acroos the state so Musk i just one of the problems facing the new Democratic governor. Neighboring New Mexico which has managed it's resources wisely in the same period under Socialism could serve as an example.

comments.name: Dalmatian Grey
comments.body: "Without those incentives, 'Tesla would be forced to further evaluate this potential investment outside of the state of Texas,' they said, according to state documents." OK first of all why do 2 companies with a combined worth of a TRILLION dollars need incentives in the form of grants and tax breaks??? That's insane.  Second, the above quote from Tesla is just the generic threat spoiled, greedy corporations always make when faced with reasonable restrictions and expectations, like paying taxes. They already uprooted and moved from California to Texas, something I'd guess took considerable resources, time, and a disruption to their business. And they've already built and are in the process of building more infrastructure in Texas so, what, you think they're really going to abandon all that and try to relocate again? Sounds like a bluff to me. And if not, if they do leave, let's consider: do companies like Tesla actually give more than they take?

comments.name: Mad Max
comments.body: It costs money to move. I sure hope Texas Democrats call Musk’s bluff. He bet big that Texas was so beholden to Republicans that they would never question the status quo. Then Trump endorsed Paxton and proved to Texas what Republicans have become. Musk doubled down only to turn his home state a deeper shade of blue. What a marvelous example of self-inflicted tragedy! Where to next? Louisiana? Florida? I think Alabama would be a safe bet. They chose a barely above-average coach for governor because he took the Tigers to the Sugar Bowl.

comments.name: SMB
comments.body: One of Talarico’s ads was about how Texas was not for sale.  I understand now what that means: $1.7 billion from Texas to Musk; a polluting, energy hungry, data center; same thing with a semiconductor plant, etc. Musk is trying to set up his own feudal lands in Texas where he makes laws, controls everything, and acts as a robber baron. And Texas paid him to do this. Look at the Nvidia disaster due to personal weaknesses at the top. A Musk mess in Texas.

comments.name: michael mccann
comments.body: So Texas republicans were stupid enough to give the richest man in the world tax breaks and other incentives? For what? How does this fiscal mismanagement benefit the citizens of Texas?

comments.name: Thomas
comments.body: I don't care. "Now what?" Oh, I don't know - maybe you'll actually be beholden to the rule of law like the rest of us?

“Tesla would be forced to further evaluate this potential investment outside of the state of Texas,”

Buh-Bye! Leave the taxes you stole on the way out.

comments.name: Norman
comments.body:
Speaking as a regular, down to earth American--

--I felt a warm glow in my heart as I read this article.  

Seems to me we saw two powerful entities at work in Texas.  

(1) Mr. Musk with billions of dollars at his disposal
(2) The electorate. They don't have billions of dollars.  

But coming together as they did--

--they administered a stunning rebuke to the billionaire.  

Oh excuse me!  The trillionaire.  A guy now possessed of upwards of $1,000,000,000,000.  A tidy sum, oh yes! 

--but we're still a democracy.  Even under Donald Trump and the Republicans that (like little dogs) jump up to do his bidding.  

But no!  I don't expect the Democrats to turn a vengeful eye upon Mr. Musk--

--whom I cannot help regarding (and please forgive my language) as a repellent human being!  

No more than they have to.  

The welfare of thousands of Texans is bound up with the man's multifarious financial concerns.  I'm sure the Dems haven't forgotten this.  Not for a moment! 

BUT--

--they are not the servile lapdogs of Elon Musk.  They weren't elected to spread out red carpets for him wherever he might choose to walk.  

They weren't elected to follow the guy around, wielding fans (so he don't get hot in all that panhandle heat)--

--or sheltering that precious head under innumerable parasols. 

They were elected to serve the people of Texas.  

And if that means working with an Elon Musk--

--what to say?  

--so be it.  

Thanks, NYT.

comments.name: LeCarre
comments.body: Reasonable thinking and move from the regime’s perspective. But the most fundamental thing for Iran is that it has no viable path to create a vibrant economy and increase living standards for its citizens. The regime will forever be under pressure from its citizens, its neighbors, and Western powers. It might get more missiles, but its citizens will stay poor.

comments.name: michjas
comments.body: This is an especially enlightening article. Without saying this explicitly, it makes it clear that Trump, his advisers, his negotiators, US intelligence, expert analysts and the New York Times are all reading tea leaves when it comes to analyzing Iran’s negotiation positions. Repeatedly, the article gives alternative views on Iran’s priorities without resolving the disputes. And how Iran will factor in the midterms in their strategy is made difficult because we don’t understand their strategy. Heck, we don’t even know who is running the country, let alone what their negotiation priorities are, what they are willing to settle for and whether they are even interested in a negotiated peace. As for what it would take to resolve what is purportedly the main issue, nuclear proliferation, that remains a question for another day.

comments.name: Bill
comments.body: TRUMP’S BIGGEST MISTAKES: “I alone can fix it” and “I always listen to my gut”. By not forming a coalition with our allies, Trump’s Iran strategy was doomed to fail. It’s not too late. If Trump was willing to regain the trust of our allies, with a global approach, increasing sanctions and protecting the Strait of Hormuz together, the coalition could hopefully be able to put enough pressure on Iran to come to the negotiating table.

comments.name: Bill McGrath
comments.body: If only the US had a strategist who could envision an end game, we might move forward. Unfortunately, we have a vain man who doesn't have the intellectual horsepower to see through to a solution. None of our adversaries see us as a formidable power. We might have a huge arsenal, but that alone cannot guarantee a favorable outcome. They see dealing with Trump as tantamount to dealing with a child. I just don't see how this will end well for the US. Thanks, MAGA.

comments.name: David Baker
comments.body: This the war which the US started and has already won according to Trump. So what is going on is the war over or not.

comments.name: Stephen
comments.body: Iran has been living with sanctions for decades. Even though a large percentage of Iranians oppose their country’s leadership and its laws that take away their rights and freedoms to live as a free human they are still a very proud and patriotic people. The Iranian heritage dates back 2.6 thousand years. Iran has excellent schools and has five prestigious universities that some of the best in the Middle East and all five rank in the world’s top one thousand best universities. Just as our own citizens would unite against another nation attacking our country. The Iranian people will do the same. Iran will outlast Trump’s navel blockade of its ports or shipping routes. In the meantime they will be rearming and rebuilding their infrastructure. Send in competent negotiators who have a knowledge of Iran’s history, culture and power dynamics that control the country and their thought process. The worst thing to do is send Witkoff and Kushner. The Iranians are highly educated and skilled negotiators. Do not send any lightweights thumping their chests and demanding they concede to our terms it would be a futile waste of time.

comments.name: riskstrategies
comments.body:
Mr Trump was in trouble in Iran even before the midterm fiasco. It is difficult to understand how Mr Netanyahu managed to persuade Mr Trump to undertake this misadventure.
Airpower alone does not win wars unless you decide to use nuclear weapons. Troops on the ground are not the answer either given US experience in Vietnam or Russian experience in Ukraine.
Sanctions also do not seem to be working given experiences in Cuba, Russia, apartheid riven South Africa or elsewhere.
On the other hand what seems to be working for Iran is it's asymmetrical approach to warfare, not a direct confrontation with the your aggressor but an attack on the aggressor's allies and supporters.
Let's not forget that Iran has been around for more than 4,000 years and this latest confrontation is merely just another event in its long history. 
Of course Iran is now emboldened .
Mr Trump is now walking around with an albatross around his neck.  Having an albatross around your neck means carrying a heavy, inescapable and persistent burden, that will destroy his sought after legacy. 
To save even a modicum of a legacy Mr Trump should declare that Iran has been taught her lesson and walk away

comments.name: Barry of Nambucca
comments.body:
Trump’s own Director of National Intelligence, wrote earlier this year, that Iran was no threat to the US.
Netanyahu has been claiming for over 30 years that Iran is just weeks away from developing nuclear weapons. No other US president took Netanyahu’s claims about Iran’s nuclear weapons seriously.
Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei issued a religious decree (fatwa) forbidding the development, production, stockpiling, and use of nuclear weapons.
The US killed Ayatollah Ali Khamenei early in the war. He was replaced by his son, who is far more hard line.
Trump never consulted Congress, the UN or long term US allies, before the US attacked Iran.
Trump is stuck in an Iran War of his making. Oil prices and inflation remain high, thanks to Trump. A face saving exit from Trump’s Iran War, still seems a long way off.

Trump cannot tolerate anyone seeing something differently from the way he does. To him, disagreement is disloyalty. He cannot conceive of the idea that there are often multiple rational ways to view a particular problem.

comments.name: Patrick
comments.body: It doesn't change the overall point (or the fact that the sketch was hilarious) but being my parents' only surviving son, I cared for my Mom hands on through almost a year of hospice, including yes, toileting, dispensing meds, appointments, right up to holding her hands as she took her last breaths. Now I'm coordinating care for my elderly father, having moved him to assisted living and acting as his power of attorney and only family support.  I don't have a sister, but man I wish I did sometimes.  All my respect to anyone who steps up to care for an aging family member.

comments.name: Theni
comments.body: Absolutely true. I have one sister, unmarried and no kids. I had to move temporarily to another town for cancer treatment. My wife could not join me since we had school going young kids. So  I would have to do the treatment along. My sister was the one who voluntarily offered her services to me and made my stay away from my own family less stressful and certainly more enjoyable considering the circumstances. I am forever grateful to her and consider myself lucky to have such a sister. BTW the skit was funny and true.

comments.name: A Texan
comments.body: You're right about the hoarding of assets.  I have to assume it will cost me a fortune to pay the caregivers I may need, so I keep more money than I need for daily life, in the bank.  I'd rather spend it now on the next generation's education and housing; but that creates an unknowable but significant risk they'll be burdened with my care in the future.  My own father solved this problem by refusing food and water, and also visits from his children.  To each his or her own.

comments.name: Michael Fiske
comments.body: My Mother at age 91, when she was tossed out of the apartment she rented from one of my sisters, chose to move halfway across country to live in a retirement home less than a mile from my home. My three younger sisters would stop by for visits about once a year.

comments.name: Na
comments.body:
I think the underlying issue is missed by the skit and many commenters: the fault is not in the brother but in the parents, who grew up and lived during the greatest time to make money in the history of the world, yet in the end did not prepare for what is completely inevitable.

They did not save for it, they did not vote for policies that would make it easier, and they did not mentally or physically prepare for it. 

Instead, they assumed children that are struggling to buy their first home, to afford health care, and to find a good school for their kids would simply become their nurse, bank, and chauffeur. 

Sisters resenting their lazy brothers is undoubtably correct, but also misses the underlying guilty party.

comments.name: DK
comments.body: When my grandmother was ailing, it was my mother, the daughter-in-law, who leapt in to help without hesitation, while my dad, the biological son, shrugged and stared helplessly on.  He is a kind person but the concept of nurturing care seemed beyond his ken.

comments.name: Ben
comments.body:
I know many situations shown on this sketch. My wife were the lead caregiver for her wheel chaired confined father where we split a lot of the care duties as well as maintained his breakeven rental property. We converted our family room into a bedroom and added a handicap shower to the downstairs bath.  

Fortunately, my parents were able to move into a life care community that provided independent living to skilled nursing.

comments.name: C
comments.body: I am the sister with two older brothers. I live the furthest away and have the youngest children. My brothers are doing all the care for our elderly mom. It breaks my heart. I wish I was there.

articles.title: That ‘S.N.L.’ Sketch About Sister? It’s More Like Nonfiction.

articles.summary: “Saturday Night Live” exposed a truth about gender roles in caring for aging parents: While many nations have a federal safety net for older adults, the U.S. has sisters.

comments.name: Ryan
comments.body:
I agree the root cause of this latest disruption should be investigated before spending a bunch of money. We should also be looking at how air traffic is being handled in other countries to see how our systems could be improved or replaced.

I would be cautious about just ripping out old systems and installing new ones without thinking about how the transition will happen. Air traffic control is already in extremely high stress high-stakes job. We really don't need to be adding fuel to that particular fire.

comments.name: Traveling cook
comments.body: Why not do some independent design reviews before mucking around in the system?  I would not want some company in the middle getting cash on transactions, able to blackmail us.  I'm thinking of Musk and Ukraine here.

comments.name: Karen C.
comments.body: Is it true that the latest $875 million system for ATC is run by Duffy's son-in-law?  Does Congress have responsibility or opportunity for oversight?  How was the money spent and what did we get?

comments.name: Avery Truitt
comments.body: Mr. Boyd, the consultant, does not mention what starting over would look like, or how it would be implemented. Is that how he makes his money, by acting as if he is the be all and end all, without having any real idea of what should be done?

comments.name: Bob
comments.body: Except for enriching himself and cronies, Trump has no plans. To expect his appointees to develop and implement plans is a waste of time and energy.

comments.name: anatlanta
comments.body:
If the Free Flight option has not been considered for 32 years, then it is not good enough for it to be sold and adopted. 

However, we should not have to wait another 32 years before we get a more modern ATC system. For example, the TPF-based flight operations systems used by Delta and United were written in the 1960s and were modernized only about 10 odd years ago. Such systems are complex and very very difficult to replace; but, it can be done. 

Wringing  hands or throwing bucket loads of money will not solve the problem - unless, of course, the aviation industry goes the way of the horse buggies or the railroads and gets replaced by AT (artificial travel) which takes away the need to travel altogether!

Short of that - we need to hire a team that has done these exact same project before and/or transplant a solution that works elsewhere and can scale.

comments.name: Stewart
comments.body:
SO the whole request for 50 billion was already determined a shakedown and here we have a private company who can't wait to get their hands on tax dollars calling for basically privatization in complete alignment with Project 2025.  

This isn't an opinion....  its gaslighting you into selling off the ATC to private equity and then watch as the service dies by slow financial strangulation ending up with the tax payer funding another government service in 20 years.

These opinions are brought to you to get you to give up as if the advice is the only option.

comments.name: Fry
comments.body: I'm not familiar with "Free Flight" but based on the author's description it sounds like turning major airports into uncontrolled airfields. That is quite literally insane.

articles.title: $50 Billion Won’t Fix Air Traffic Control. It Needs to Be Scrapped.
articles.summary: The transportation secretary wants to pour more dollars into an obsolete structure, much like upgrading a Model T for a highway.

comments.name: Fisher
comments.body: “I’d like to see Democrats come up with a credible replacement for USAID.”  While no agency is perfect, USAID did a lot of good at a relatively low cost.  The USAID budget hovered around $20B for years, then crept up in ‘21-‘23 to the $40B range due to COVID I suspect.  (www.wheremytaxesgo.com/usaid/). The bulk of the USAID budget was for humanitarian aid, health responses and economic development with sub-Saharan Africa the largest recipient.  While $20B is a lot of money, it is spare change compared to what we spend elsewhere.  What do we get for our money, at least grudging respect for the U.S. and some mitigation of our otherwise rather poor reputation in the developing world.  Soft power works, I have seen it all over the world.  Rename USAID if it is politically necessary but restoring funding to past levels is essential and would demonstrate to the world that we in the U.S. are not all rapacious war-mongering tyrants.

comments.name: John Ondespot
comments.body:
Trump lost this war of choice on the second day.  Over.  Done.  Stupid.

Hegseth lost it before we even got a start.

On the other hand, I sort of wish Don would hang about the old straight for a while.  That way he might leave Cuba alone which, despite predjudiced polls asserting otherwise, the Cuban people would clearly prefer.

We owe them that much, at least.

The Great Iranian Campaign will end when Iran says it's over.

comments.name: Jonathan
comments.body:
Boiling down these exchanges to the following specific actions proposed:

1.  Impeach Hegseth. [Proceed if there is a decent chance of conviction in the Senate]
2.  Legislation to limit Iran war funding to defense of US personnel, shipping and our allies in the region. [An important statement, even though Trump will veto]
3.  Oversight Hearings on Administration covert operations, particularly in the Western Hemisphere. [Not an immediate priority]
4.  Summon top Administration officials to explain their plans for Cuba. [Important policy matter; not a major issue concerning voters]
5. Legislation to force Administration to supply Ukraine with available interceptors. [Important policy matter; not a major issue concerning voters]
6. Investigate Starlink and the relationship between Musk, the Pentagon, and Ukraine.  [Important policy matter; not a major issue concerning voters]
7. Investigate actual and proposed transactions between Russia and its affiliates and Trump's allies. [Pick one of the corruption issues to illustrate the rot in this Administration. This may be it.]
8.  Legislate as necessary to return the tariff power to Congress. and begin the necessary steps to reduce and or eliminate destructive tariffs. [Should be a top priority.]
9.  Choose Chris Van Hollen as Senate majority leader.  [Van Hollen is 67 years old. He's been in Congress since 2003. He is just a slightly younger insider, establishment politician. This is not the generational change Democrats need.]

comments.name: John Fraser
comments.body: To end the war in Iran, Cuban violation of international law and a humanitarian war crime, and the war crimes and piracy at sea, Congress needs to make clear that the war is unauthorized and these are illegal orders for which all military members participating or following orders will be subject to criminal trial.  Furthermore, because they are illegal orders, the President does not enjoy immunity and nor can he use his pardon power because it benefits him directly.  Allow 30 days to cease operations in Iran but otherwise, as of the date of the resolution, 24 hours to end to blockade of Cuba.   That would be clear and decisive.  Follow that with impeachment of Hegseth and send a warning to the joint chiefs that their complicity was against the law and subject to independent tribunal.  Sure, they may say lots of bad things but this is one place where the SCOTUS may actually grow a spine.

comments.name: RickP
comments.body:
Trump will be constrained if and when 10 Senators flip and signal a willingness to convict in an impeachment trial - of Trump. 

This may not be possible, but here is a path that seems promising. 

Focus on the most egregious illegal behavior that can be identified.  I'd suggest the sale of pardons. Catch him red-handed and trumpet it far and wide. Force the MAGA Senators to support clear criminal behavior, or flip.  Confront any MAGA lies or spin - and keep at it.

comments.name: Kathy
comments.body: Russell Vought and Stephan Miller are the first two who need to go. They are behind Project 25 and picked Trump to be the puppet to make it happen. Trump has been their perfect figurehead. Every thing, other than his "beautification of Washington D.C.", has been the plan of Project 25. Many of the contributors to it are also now part of the administration. Although I consider myself a Democrat, I truly believed the Republicans in congress would step up and uphold our Constitution. Maybe if Vought and Miller were no longer in power some of them would remember the reason they were elected.

comments.name: Brent Schaeffer
comments.body: Glad to see Calabresi offer support for a new USAID, but his nuanced support -- "[USAID] had serious problems — even their staunchest supporters admit" -- would have been more informative had it acknowledged that many of those serious problems reflected USAID staff's struggle to implement inappropriate Congressional mandates.

comments.name: Lawrence Lewis
comments.body: Our allies in the Persian Gulf are being attacked for only one reason. The US and Israel chose to attack Iran without provocation! Unproven claims of uranium enrichment is not a valid reason for an all-out bombing assault and sea blockage of international trade.

articles.title: ‘It’s Easier Said Than Done’: 3 Opinion Writers on How to Check Trump

articles.summary: Presidents usually have wide latitude on foreign policy. Will the next Congress change that?

comments.name: M
comments.body:
So some plain speak for people that play games and aren't GTA defenders or evangelists: 

"It’s all impressively done and rendered with technological aplomb, but it isn’t anything we haven’t seen before. Instead, the game’s artistry is felt most in its Bonnie and Clyde duo."

Got it. Doesn't revolutionize gameplay or anything, just new city and leads with better graphics. Video games are 100% art but this sequel feels more Avengers: Endgame than Aliens.

comments.name: Norman
comments.body:
Years ago, I taught down in Philly.  In a private high school.

And I told the kids I'd never in my life played a video game.  

They looked at me as if I'd never seen a flush toilet.  

But I hear things about this Grand Theft Auto.  Not nice things.  

Torture?  Is there a scene depicting some wretched guy being tortured?  By having his teeth extracted--

--shades of "The Mikado."  

                  "His teeth I've enacted
                    Shall all be extracted
                        By terrified amateurs."  

Or am I mixed up?  Confusing this with something else.  

But in any case, this picture of a young couple learning love and commitment--

--by robbing people and carrying on general mayhem--

--caught (as it were) in the throes of a rat tat tat passion.  Snatching kisses while wielding a tommy gun--

--no!  Sorry.  Not to my taste.  

To be frank, it sounds a bit creepy.  

Very creepy in fact.  

Thanks, NYT.

comments.name: What
comments.body: Ah, nothing like the concept of "Grand Theft Auto" stealing your heart. The picture of a woman shooting gun, apparently trying to run away from some other violent act, that really does make one think of love, relationships and nurturing.

comments.name: Mixilplix
comments.body:
Seriously. An entire set piece about painting a house?
That's like a Simpsons episode where Bart gets a lousy game.

comments.name: Mixilplix
comments.body: GTA was always about Americans goofing on American Culture. Once you make is sweet and profound, you lose the DNA that made it so brilliant.

comments.name: Greener
comments.body: To paraphrase an ancient Twitter meme, "Everything I know about GTA I've learned against my will."

comments.name: JE
comments.body: If video games aren’t your thing, that’s fine. No need to comment on those who do like them. Different strokes for different folks.

comments.name: Betsy Handler
comments.body: Seen on a bus I was stuck behind. A large ad for GTA, and below, in small text, “ Intense violence, blood and gore, drug use, strong language.” Disgusting.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI Will Steal Your Heart
articles.summary: The series matures beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups with a game about love, relationships and nurturing your partner.

comments.name: Mike
comments.body: I think part of the issue is extreme wealth inequality. Communities are stretched thin and look for ways to get more money as services get more expensive giving corporations increasing control. When your example of benefits is of common customers being a single mother too busy and exhausted to get diapers for their baby- there's more than just a speedy delivery problem.

comments.name: Times Reader 1978
comments.body: I am so grateful to the Times for this story. I has heard  about these drones but did not realize they were in full force in so many places. Being very sensitive to noise, I  know that if this horror show started in my neighborhood I would soon completely lose my mind. I can't believe the people who are or will be the victims of this blight will not eventually force an end to it. I foresee the protests being overwhelming--at least I hope they will be. It is absolutely insane that Amazon has been allowed to start doing this with so few guardrails and I hope enough citizens unite and act to stop it. I'm contacting my town about it and urge others to do the same.

comments.name: Scope1
comments.body: For a moment, let's adopt the "David and Goliath" narrative: Amazon is of course the Goliath in this stroy, and the good people of Westborough, MA, and other affected municipalities are David. As I recall, a slingshot and a well-placed rock took the Goliath out. I know that FAA regulations rule out the slignshot AND YET, it seems that some form of oppositional tactics are in order. I thik Amazon should be prepared for some version of mass revolt, maybe in the form of a civic boycott, but maybe with a few pointers from good old David of yore.

comments.name: Anna Key
comments.body:
In a country awash in guns, I don’t see this drone thing ending well.  Just look what Kid Rock did to beer cans.  
Also impoverishing as many people as possible in a country awash in guns isn’t going to end well either (that includes for those of us who don’t own guns).

comments.name: Isthisreallyamerica
comments.body: People need to realize what the the opening of the skies to drone delivery really means; it is the end of your quiet backyard; the end of your ability to enjoy that peace and quiet by yourself or with your family or friends; the end of your right to enjoy a peaceful environment at home away from work and maybe, the big city. They already are ripping up the country for data centers we didn’t ask for or want, further polluting the air and increasing energy costs. Now they want to tear up the skies and make sure they further ruin our ability to live a peaceful life, all to save Bezos money(because, you know he isn’t rich enough). Say NO to drone delivery. If Amazon gets this, it means all delivery businesses get it. And if that happens, we all truly lose!

comments.name: akamai
comments.body:
I am thrilled to read this.  How could anyone think drones would not be noisy and spying?

Drones should be a non-starter anywhere.

I'll bet Bezos doesn't let drones fly over his mansionS.

This, of course, is blue Massachusetts.  Will Red States override the will of the people?

comments.name: Nan
comments.body: Good for them. May this become the new normal.

comments.name: Robert Rosenthal
comments.body: Three cheers for the residents of Marlborough.  In standing up for their quality of life they demonstrated that it is possible to "slay the dragon."

Brovdi has mastered another part of his tech-chief role: a bullish social-media presence.

comments.name: Burt B

comments.name: WalksInPortland
comments.body: As someone born in Alaska in 1955 who lived there until 1986, I was delighted by Mary Peltola’s victory. Congratulations to Senator-elect Peltola, and congratulations to the people of Alaska for making this choice. It’s wonderful to see Alaska represented by someone who has earned the confidence of its citizens.

comments.name: Martin
comments.body: Progressives versus moderates, Democrats versus Republicans. This fighting is what the powerful and rich are setting up. Until the broken political system is fixed, there will be little real change.

comments.name: Spruce
comments.body: After living in Alaska for decades then experiencing  Sullivan and Gov Dunleavy policies for the past eight years, I am hopeful and thankful Mary won the senate and JKT is the new governor. Both Dunleavy and Sullivan did nothing for the average Alaskan. The ferry system, schools, every state agency was adversely affected by their leadership. I left state employment along with many others as a result of their policies and saw first hand how the average person was affected. I am hopeful for a brighter future and glad to see young vibrant leaders.

comments.name: Flaminia
comments.body:
It's been really interesting and refreshing to watch the variety of successful Democratic candidates in states not known for Democratic electoral success in recent years/decades.  One of the relatively consistent attributes is that these successful candidates have run on issues relevant to their local voters who will now be their constituents.  This is something that both major parties' leaders have forgotten.  

I'm a lifelong Democrat but even so I think a healthy government needs two successful and viable competing parties.  I've been arguing for years now that Republicans will enjoy electoral success here in California when they finally pay attention to the local electorate and craft policies relevant to them.  The issues and proposed solutions relevant to Republicans in places like Kansas and Alabama are not remotely relevant to Californians. 

It's great to see these grassroots level Democrats sidestep the nationalization of party politics.  I hope the party leaders take the hint.  Yes we are all citizens of one nation but we are not homogeneous and our regions have their own pressing issues.

comments.name: Jeff Kassel
comments.body: High costs are here to stay because we've got serious inflation due to a botched war in Iran who is still destroying ships in the Persian Gulf. Inflation is built in with a $40.5 trillion dollar federal debt and interest costs on that debt built in and rising to $1.5 trillion this year as $8 trillion of old debt is rolled over at much higher rates. Congress can do little about higher costs and unaffordability, especially as workers lose jobs to AI.

comments.name: Gina
comments.body: This was a repudiation election. It wasn't just the economy. People were sending a strong message to Trump and the GOP that corruption, the Iran war, cronyism, tariffs, election tampering, etc., will not be tolerated. And it also was an election where Democrats put up remarkably good candidates who listened to the voters.

comments.name: Daniel Shapiro
comments.body:
Daniel Shapiro | Suffern NY
Consistent with the choices they’ve made over the last ten years, the Democrats have once again failed to listen to the electorate. Instead of effecting the significant change the voters indicated they wanted in government, the House Democratic establishment stayed with the same leadership that has garnered them a public favorability rating of under 30%. Apparently the Democratic establishment doesn’t understand and/or refuses to accept that the election mandated change and an overwhelming rejection of the Republican party as well as significant policy changes, not an approval of the current Democratic Party leadership.  The voters want change, not the same leadership from the Democrats that was a spectacular failure as an opposition party to Trumpism during the last two and a half years.

comments.name: Mary
comments.body: As an Alaskan, I am relieved I will not have to read another skewed Kellen Browning story about Mary Peltola. Kellen, did you not know how hammered Alaskans were by the hateful and unrelenting Dan Sullivan attack ads aired on TV here calling Peltola a liar? Did you not see the debate where Sullivan couldn't answer the questions and accused Peltola of cheating because she came prepared? Kellen, maybe visit Alaska. Peltola resonated on the issues. That's why she won.

articles.title: Fish and High Prices: How Mary Peltola Triumphed in Alaska’s Senate Race
articles.summary: Beleaguered by high fuel costs and wary of overfishing, Alaskans were drawn to the Democrat’s hyperlocal pitch.

comments.name: Wishful Thinking
comments.body:
Well I am not surprised, Trump was
banking there too at one point. Is he still?

comments.name: Whip or Will
comments.body: I seem to remember some questionable situation with this bank employing the son of one of our former Supreme Court justices.  Was it Kennedy?

comments.name: hapinoregon
comments.body: Why am I NOT surprised? Deutsche Bank's fiscal/social history the past 100 years or so does not lend itself to good feelings and thoughts.

comments.name: ChristopherWyvill
comments.body: Yet further evidence that "business ethics" is an oxymoron.

comments.name: Scope1
comments.body: Money can sometimes be like a snail...leaving a slimy but discernible trail wherever it has crawled. Following the money, while never more complicated than it is today (with intangible/immaterial funds, technological concealment, and unprecedented speed of transfer...not snail-like at all) is still possible. The leak at the core of this story is another example of how such details gradually emerge. The question then is whether there is the will, power, and legal structure to hold oligarchs and criminal opportunists to account for their gross malfeasance.

comments.name: 304th Vet
comments.body: Deutsche Bank should be forced to disband.  They persistently and  consistently have been found to be willing participants in money laundering.  They are a corrupt business that needs to be hammered.

comments.name: Lulu
comments.body:
Believe it or not, there are thousands of descendants of the Commodore around, and a great deal of them are not wealthy!  My Vanderbilt ancestress married a man who did his best to lose every Vanderbilt penny that was not tied down.  Any small bit of inherited money is due to decent marriages, nothing Vanderbilt!  

Biltmore is a huge success due to intelligent and thoughtful leadership. The wine they make is good, for example. The recent tragic flooding of Asheville largely destroyed the many houses built for the workers by that Vanderbilt. Houses that lasted and were occupied by many people!  Asheville was lovely and I hope it recovers. Biltmore will be a huge part of the recovery. The people who live there truly care about their community.

comments.name: Ivy Hilliard
comments.body: I wish that magnificent house could have been preserved and Bergdorfs put inside it, or like the Henry Clay Frick home, a museum full of the house's art.  The Frick Museum is a remarkable preservation. of an era, and its opulence.

comments.name: David Loiterman
comments.body:
Architectural preservation is a subjective " Art " and requires the custodians to exhibit judgement, a sense of history and culture.

Anyone who has travelled through the " Great Cities " of Europe will understand. It is impossible to preserve every structure and selecting the best examples of a particular style and time window is a skill that is both valuable and hard to teach.

Thank you to the NYT for this insightful story

comments.name: CWF
comments.body: It seems odd to chastise a house for being built in a neighborhood that won't suit it decades from now. This was an incredible example of craftsmanship that we don't see in buildings anymore. We don't really have tradespeople who can produce work like this anymore. Once it's gone, it's gone. In the northeast we often see 18th & 19th cen. homes close to a busy highway that seem out of place, but that was simply the main road through town 150 years ago. I'm glad they're still there. Sure beats a data center and a starbucks.

comments.name: Craig Purcell
comments.body: I wonder what a comparable “Modern” style would look like as it celebrated abstractions as language.

comments.name: Charles
comments.body: Looking down Fifth Avenue at a current Google street view image of that same intersection, it is daunting to realize that not a single building appears to remain from that time (c. 1900).  The old reality has been completely wiped out and only survives in artifacts and photographs.  Can we presume this will happen to the current scene as well?

comments.name: Kristie
comments.body: What a tremendous waste of materials and labor to  tear down this guilded age house. Imagine all the trees and steel and environmental damage done just to build this house. For it to be torn down just 33 years later is an abomination. The house would have made an incredible Bergdorfs department store. Instead, it was all just wasted. America, and NY especially, has a terrible habit of doing just this. We don't seem to value much of hard work or money spent or beauty. Just pave it over and put up a parking lot, right? It also would have made an incredible museum. Thank god the Frick was saved for this purpose.

comments.name: jeff willaims
comments.body: Wonderful article. Thank you.

articles.title: When the Vanderbilts’ Gilded Age Mansion Was Razed for Retail
articles.summary: Just over 100 years ago, the Cornelius Vanderbilt II House was demolished to make way for Bergdorf Goodman. Today, remnants of the estate are scattered around the city.

comments.name: Susan
comments.body: The Times should have noted that Peltola had 144,302 votes.  The total number of votes from the two Sullivans' and Heikes totaled 142,709.

comments.name: Shirley Marquez
comments.body:
I didn't think Peltola would reach a clear majority, and it seemed likely that activating the ranked choice process would shift the balance to Dan S Sullivan. (The votes for the other Republican, Heikes, seemed likely to go there, as were the votes for the other Dan Sullivan.) But it happened.

So we will have a very clear Democratic majority in the Senate term from 2026 to 2028, though not enough to break a filibuster. This election is about as good a result for them as could realistically be achieved. It will be enough to stop Trump from doing much legislatively, though the Democrats will struggle to pass laws because Trump will have the veto pen at the ready.

comments.name: Snow
comments.body: It should be noted that Peltola would have won even if you gave all the votes from one Dan Sullivan to another.

comments.name: AAF
comments.body: Congratulations! Now the hard part part for all the newly elected Democrats, delivering on the campaign promises.

comments.name: LH

comments.name: Hal's Friend
comments.body:
I share in the congratulation to the new  Democratic Senator from Alaska 
However the 2nd Dan Sullivan on the ballot stunt does not speak well for her or her team

comments.name: Professor
comments.body: Hold on.  I thought the Justice Department said the election result would only be legitimate if the Republiczn won.

comments.name: F
comments.body:
This is great news. Congratulations to Mary Peltola. 
If only all Democrats were immediately in office. I’m just afraid of what Trump, Miller, Blanch, and the rest of the  amoral incompetents will destroy before we can boot them out. We know Republicans simply enable every horrible decision Trump makes.

comments.name: jhurwich
comments.body: I never use Google Search (or any other Google feature, if I can help it) because I don't want them to collect my data. I recommend DuckDuckGo, which doesn't collect cookies.

comments.name: Brian V
comments.body:
I really don't know why it hasn't been a part of digital literacy training for decades now to discuss search engine alternatives and why you might want to change from one to the other or use one versus another selectively.

I stopped using Google Search many years ago, but am still a loyal Gmail user and use the Gemini AI chatbot as its own function with some frequency (along with Perplexity.ai, and Copilot, primarily, and occasional use of Claude and ChatGPT).  An AI Chatbot is a different tool than a good, "old-fashioned" search engine.

I switched to the DuckDuckGo search engine many years ago now.  Definitely more than a decade ago.  I also use Duck.ai when I want as close as I can get to private AI chatbot interactions.

I was always taught, first in the world of physical tools, to choose my tool based upon the task it's needed to perform.  Cyber tools are no different.

comments.name: Ezra Fox
comments.body: What about Startpage? It has an option specifically for schools. And it's very similar to Google, so the switch would be easy. Anyway, I do think Google may have overplayed its hand here. Let's hope

comments.name: Barry C
comments.body:
Don't weigh it. Do it. Google does evil, contrary to its original mission statement.

Besides, Big Tech needs to be tethered. It should have no standing to dictate educational standards.

comments.name: RK
comments.body: Foundational human skills—like empathy, critical thinking, and resilience—are the essence of what our education system should be about, no different than Ancient Greek education goals, and these grow best through real-world struggle and human relationships rather than by AI use and machine interactions. In today’s world with the loss of social capital, diminishing relationships, and decreasing mental health state of our nation’s youth, let’s not confuse what is important.

comments.name: Tyler
comments.body: I say this as a software engineer.... why do there have to be computers in the classroom at all? These kids will be using computers their entire working lives. An hour of computer instruction should be enough -- some programming, spreadsheets, etc. You don't need so much exposure to computers at such a young age. I learned in my twenties back in the 1990s. It's sad that students don't have notebooks and textbooks like when I grew up. And how do they doodle?

comments.name: MM
comments.body: Yes, I am down for this! I for one have no idea why any child under the age of 10 is on any kind of digital device during the schoolday, even if it's "just a few minutes." It's not even supported by neuro-scientific research into learning approaches. The best way for kids to learn is by reading and writing by hand. Dumping this line item for schools would also enable us to divert spend into enriching extracurriculars, tutoring, and special education support.

comments.name: Steve
comments.body: The legendary John Henry was said to have died with hammer in hand, trying to prove that the human heart was more durable than the mechanical steam shovel. Do not withhold cutting-edge tools; they elevate the launchpad, situating students to attain greater heights, according to their individual aptitudes.

articles.title: U.S. School Districts Weigh Breaking Up With Google Search Over A.I.
articles.summary: Google’s refusal to unbundle A.I. features from search for students prompted a backlash. Now schools are looking for alternatives.

articles.title: Nvidia Reports Faster Growth, Says Jensen Huang Won’t Return as CEO
articles.summary: In her first earnings call as interim CEO, Colette Kress faced questions over the chipmaker’s future without its longtime leader.

comments.name: John Hillert
comments.body: Am I the only one who thinks it's freakishly weird. To designate something a national security threat and then the company just pays the government and the government "oh never mind, it's fine, sell those h200 chips"?    It's like cheating on a diet only the consequences are science fiction horror.

comments.name: Gene Kor
comments.body: Lots of talent at Nvidia are leaving. I know robotics and CUDA senior developers left. I think without Huang Nvidia will slowly fade and talent knows that. China and Japan had a soccer game in Beijing. As usual, many fans from the two countries waved big national flags to support their players. However, some Japanese waved not the present Japanese national flag but the "many-rayed" sun flag that is historically associated with the Japanese military during World War II. There followed a riot, and some Japanese stores, etc., were damaged. Japanese wondered how the Chinese could be so "uncivilized."

Imagine if at a Germany-Poland soccer game, some German fans brought swastika flags and proudly waved them around. I imagine that some German players and fans would not have made it back alive to their home country.

Aside from some academics and intellectuals, Japanese do not feel much if any remorse for the war. We Americans lost around 110,000 soldiers fighting the Japanese in the Pacific and Asia. Many thousands more suffered and died in brutal Japanese POW camps. 

China might be a threat to US security interests; but the Japanese ruling class and many of its people are not our friends.

comments.body: While the idea of making Rikers more safe is perhaps commendable, the larger issue is that while Rikers is an extreme example of inhumane and unconstitutional treatment, the jail system itself, even when well-implemented, tends toward inhumane and unconstitutional treatment. Case in point: many of the people imprisoned in Rikers share the same unfair detention as those in other, “better” jails, namely indefinite incarceration without any meaningful proof of criminal activity or specific court date. Many people whose charges are ultimately dismissed spend more time in jail, awaiting trial, than they would in prison if convicted. Of course, we should ensure jails are safer and more humane, but we also should recognize that folks accused of crimes - particularly those who are not white - generally spend excessive time in jails awaiting trial, despite supposedly being innocent until proven guilty. It is also cheaper for taxpayers and municipalities, and more likely to result in rehabilitation rather than recidivism (and support community wellbeing), to expand supervised parole rather than keep people in jail for extended periods.

My dentist had a jaguar. Somehow I knew that was his car. I was going to see if this would be a match, and indeed it turned out to be getting a root canal 4 to 5 hours. Alan - charismatic, the root canal was done by a dentist with very small fingers. I had five or six rubber dams. This was the first for me. Allan kept checking on me. The third time he came in, I asked him why he was a dentist. He said that when he was with his dad and the two of them working on the road together, and his dad said to him, Allan if you become a dentist, a doctor, or a lawyer your life will be paved in gold. The next time I came in, I said, how old were you when that happened. He said 14 years. Liar I thought to myself. This was confirmed when he called me up that night and left a message that went on for about two minutes. This is my cell phone and you can call me anytime. Yep. comments.name: GCA
comments.body: I believe it depends on the level of fitness and age. Way, way back in high school, I played football. During pre-season training, I could tell on a Monday after a weekend of less activity that Monday’s drills were noticeably harder. By Wednesday, I was back to “normal.” Running wind sprints on Saturday and Sunday helped with that. Fifty years later, as a fit ~70-year-old active person with above-average VO2 max, I seem to lose a much lower level of fitness in the same 2-3 days, and it takes two or more weeks of work to get back to where I was.

comments.name: John

I personally work out with a PhD level trainer twice a week, Monday and Fridays, and do a little extra upper body stuff on my own, on Wednesdays. I've got a Peloton bike which I've been ignoring, but will get back on sooner or later. If you are awake 16 hours a day, that's 112 hours a week. To get in really solid shape, with the right routines, would take possibly five hours a week, including the cardio work. Very much worth the time, especially as you get old. Mr. Cassidy wrote. “My conversations with her convinced me she would follow the science and push back against decisions that put Americans’ health at risk.”

He said exactly the same thing about RFK Jr.  How many times can one man make the same mistake??

He has squandered all of his credibility as a physician and as a senator.

comments.name: David
comments.body: Even the Republicans' Overton window hasn't stretched out enough to vote for this FDA nominee.

comments.name: Holly
comments.body: It's unfortunate a humane and science-supporting person can't be found to fill this vital federal role. But then when crass ideology and obstinance fuel the nomination/appointment process, what can we expect? January can't come too soon.

comments.name: James
comments.body: “The president’s interest is in the best outcomes for the American people,” she said. This comment alone makes Overton unqualified to be in any leadership position involving health care.

comments.name: John Lambert
comments.body: I tend to think experts who know better and who take obviously false stands against proven facts come in two packages.  For example, Trump (and no president) is per se correct about science and vaccines because he "cares about the American people."  This is ridiculous.  There are others who are just informed by their religious beliefs.  In either case, these people should not have any job of any consequence regarding the health of our nation.

comments.name: Matt
comments.body: Since it looks like all nominees for these Trump positions lie, any statement to support vaccines should be regarded as lip service. What we need are policies with teeth. No public school for unvaccinated children, incentives for vaccinating or repercussions for failure to do so. We live in a society, and the actions of individuals affect everyone so unless you want to be a hermit in some log cabin, playalong.

comments.name: Ahna

comments.name: Harry

comments.name: Kyle
comments.body: Does Cummings come up with these references or is it the work of a team of writers?

comments.name: Wolfy Amadeus Mole
comments.body: This superb article is a reader's adventure and a wonderful panoply of British literature. It favors drama and poetry yet is wide ranging with oft-quoted lines. They have stuck in many an avid reader's brain. Another great writer, often quoted, could be that polymath of stories, and Alan's fellow Scot: Robert Louis Stevenson. And Dickens too was very quotable. The great writers of that region made English language more than universal. All of us should be grateful for the gift.

comments.name: Tara
comments.body: I love The Traitors so much. I'm still a few eps behind in this current season (I prefer to binge three or four at a time) but this show has everything: an amazing host in Alan, his gorgeous wardrobe, and campy, tongue-in-cheek humor, beautiful cinematography, a stunning castle, drama and competition... It's just on a different level than other reality shows. I will say, though, the editing this season has been pretty rough. Maybe it's just a Peacock stream thing, but when and where they've chosen to end (and begin) episodes has left a lot to be desired. Regardless, this show is definitely Emmy-worthy.

comments.name: NOTwokeNORmaga

I guess at a certain point we should just hand over our entire paychecks to the medical industrial complex and call it good.  The industry would still not be satisfied, and would want another $40 trillion borrowed on their behalf.

comments.name: Jeff Byrnes

comments.name: Mike C.

Measles, which American doctors helped pretty much eradicate in places like Asia and Africa (which killed millions) with vaccines, is now back in the US, thanks to the stupidity of these nutjobs. MAGA/MAHA - get lost and don't come back
