comments.name: Padre
comments.body: It’s all madness. Bring all armies home, invest in education, food production, healthcare. Look after the welfare of your citizens. Don’t invade your neighbours and murder civilians. Co-operate with your neighbours, work together for the benefit of all- be peaceful and look after your interests peacefully.

comments.name: Chin
comments.body:
Very good. 
If these cheaper air defence drones/systems are more effective against the jet-powered drones and missiles, then Musk may just go away.

comments.name: MOI
comments.body: Meanwhile, back at home, trump is fiddling as Rome burns and the GOP is more concerned about who's using what bathroom and/or just enriching themselves.

comments.name: WG
comments.body: And why aren’t we doing this kind of innovation?  Maybe because Hegseth fired the people whose job it was to modernize our defense systems?  Every day that Trump and his inept cabinet are in power sets us back years in our ability to defend ourselves and compete in the world. They all need to go as soon as possible and bring back truly competent and smart people.

comments.name: dsws
comments.body:
Defenses are worth using as long as they're cheaper than what they're defending.  They're viable as long as the cost ratio is at least as favorable as the ratio of what attacker can afford versus what the defender can.  

The aggressor is a third-rate regional power.  It has a dictator who dreams of global empire, but an economy about the size of Italy's and an aging population decimated by deaths of despair.  Europe could afford to defend itself even if the shot exchange ratio were massively in the enemy's favor.  But the cheapest way for Europe to defend itself against the tsar-wannabe's attacks is to fund Ukraine's war effort, especially the deep-strike campaign against Russian logistics, so well that the oblasts bordering Ukraine can be severed from the moribund empire and turned into a prosperous normal country.

comments.name: Scott
comments.body: Another unintended consequence of Trump's bluster and tariffs.  Europeans working hard to build sophisticated weapons that are cheaper than what we can make.  They will no longer be hostage to our government or our military industrial complex. Over time how many tens of billions will have been lost to our economy?

comments.name: Cap’n Man Datthews
comments.body: Right.  And no, Air Force, you don’t need more $100 million fighter airplanes, you need more $1000 drones.

So, the 3 people watching broadcast television saw it and were alarmed? (Sorry for the snark.)

It did made me wonder if there is any kind of similar federal alert for streaming services.

comments.name: slime2
comments.body:

If we wish to make it softer, we will tune it to a whisper. We will control the horizontal. We will control the vertical. We can roll the image, make it flutter. Given that American is at war and facing severe weather impacts from El Niño and global warming, reasonable people agree that the Emergency Alert System should be tested much more frequently.

comments.name: TKNY
comments.body: Airport lounge: Tell your friends before you go to the airport that you will meet them at the gate.  It’s one thing to plan to meet at the gate, another to go to the airport with your friends and then say ‘OK, we’re off to the lounge!’ and leave them.

comments.name: Kate
comments.body: My husband and I are both 81.  Our bodies and brains are failing. Our sons live far away and never phone to see how we are doing.  We laugh and say how glad we are to be left alone, without either of them making a "plan" to direct our lives and take away our volition and control (such as it is).  Leave grandpa alone. Maybe that's how he wants it, and at this point in his life, he is entitled to that.  Now and then, check in with him and ask how he feels he is doing and ask if there is anything you can do.  Don't use Thanksgiving as an opportunity to gang up on the poor guy.

comments.name: Etc.
comments.body: For LW1, I presume one or more family members are traveling, making Thanksgiving a rare occasion for everyone to meet as a group. If that's the case, why not have a family meeting over breakfast on Friday following a joyful celebration. This will be helpful for a couple of reasons: First, the Thanksgiving meal should hopefully serve as a reminder that the family loves Grandpa and is there to help; and second, many people with dementia/Alzheimers "sundown" towards the end of the day and are not at their best.

comments.name: Vaer
comments.body:
The response regarding the nude negatives confuse me. They all seem to focus on whether the child should tell the parents about them. Presumably, the parents already know they exist. One took them and the other posed for them. So either they will deal with them or the child will deal  with them after they are gone. 
At some point if there's discussion about what will happen when they are both gone, the child could say something like maybe you should go through your things to get rid of anything you don't want to be discovered when you're gone.

comments.name: Louisa718bk
comments.body:
LW1 should hire a geriatric care manager to consult with the sibling group. Hire someone who hopefully is either well acquainted with resources in the FIL area or wherever the family expects to eventually move him to. An experienced professional will have ways of potentially approaching the FIL, and/or helping the kids see the path ahead and how to prepare for it.  

One showdown will NOT produce the desired result. It took my siblings and I over two years to get our widowed stepmother suffering dementia across the country and resettled in a residential community. We started with a (unfortunately limited) Power of Attorney, but it helped once we had a doctor’s letter.  We have never had to do anything against her will, and have allowed her to FEEL independent even though we are managing every single thing. 

There is a lot involved, and most families are 24-36 months behind where the aging parent really needs to be. Good luck to them, and get some help/insight.

comments.name: Marzocco
comments.body: I am confused by letter #1. Quite apart from mental decay, how could any one person, not to mention someone in his seventies, run a farm by himself? I am quite the city person myself but I do know that a farm means strenuous physical labor. Isn't a plan to relieve him of this labor overdue anyway, dementia or no dementia?

comments.name: Memphis Vivian
comments.body:
THANKSGIVING,
Have your husband and his siblings discussed the situation among themselves, in depth, and formed at least a rudimentary plan? They all need to be on the same page before any one of them brings up the situation with their father. If not, Thanksgiving is just too soon. And BTW, they  should NOT have those discussions over Thanksgiving either — odds are pretty good your FIL will be hyper alert to the possibility that he is being talked about, and become more stubborn and defensive.

comments.name: Karen
comments.body: LW4 - We travel a lot with friends and family, and the best way to enjoy the experiences is to not be together every minute. Go to the lounge, enjoy yourself, and meet them at the gate. No biggie.

articles.summary: A reader asks whether there’s any way to keep a conversation about her father-in-law’s worsening Alzheimer’s disease from torpedoing her plans for a joyful holiday.

comments.name: Lemon Lemur
comments.body: At Balthazar they give a free glass of bubbly to every lady eating alone. A waiter told me that policy was set by Mr. McNally himself from day one. Smart and kind! Balthazar has soul.

comments.name: MG
comments.body: Hate to be a predictable boomer, but I remember: the Odeon in the 80's, just walk in and it was a scene - drink, eat - but you could just walk in! And of course Puffy's, Yaffa's, El Teddy's, Montrachet etc were real neighborhood joints. Now Tribeca is the most exclusive of anywhere in the city. And they have Nepo-Faux too!

comments.body: Sometimes a restaurant reviewer has to be bruising, but the blows here are not landing. Similar to the "Alinea" review. I admire Ms.Mishan's positive reviews but the take-downs are like feather-pokes. Not much fun to read. High time to really sharpen the dagger.

comments.name: Hal
comments.body: Whenever the review is less than stellar, or worse (like this one!), I feel a little sad for the happy, chatting patrons in the video. Do they read the review, see themselves enjoying mediocre fare and feel foolish? Defensive? Caught in a compromising position? Probably not. They're probably above it all. Still, I think it might be a little unsettling. I wonder mostly if it makes them revise their opinion of their outing? In any case, it must be much more fun to the unwitting stars in the videos of fabulous places where everyone wants to be; you're the envy of others then, not the butt of humor and disdain.

comments.name: Gregg
comments.body: I'd go here for a drink, order a bite at the bar and enjoy the scene. Sounds lively and fun. But wait..is there a bar you can hang out at and chill or is it a service bar? Inquiring minds want to sloshy

comments.name: kathy

comments.body: My first thought was why they didn’t consider a young black actor. There are plenty of them that would be great in the part.

comments.name: Steve Paradis
comments.body:
Ever go through the channels and land upon a show that you thought was canceled years ago? And there they are, still going through the same old stuff.
That's Bond. 
You'd have thought that Sam Neill's turn as the real James Bond in "Reilly: Ace of Spies" would have put the whole thing to bed, but the zombie franchise just keeps rolling along.

comments.name: Ben Calwell
comments.body: Speaking of “manly gravitas,” I always thought Pierce Brosnan’s 007 was lacking in that department. To my eye, his features and manner were a little too delicate for the role.

comments.name: Ken Burk
comments.body:
Isn’t this what was promised from casting Timothy Dalton? A grittier antihero rather than the loveable rogue that was Roger Moore? 
It didn’t work. It won’t work this time. Bond can’t be an antihero because he has to be the bastion against an antihero. The best Bond villains are the ones who aren’t 2D demons and have an alternate agenda with a tinge of being a psychopath.

comments.name: Canute
comments.body:
The postcolonial messaging isn’t front and center for most viewers. They just want a non-boring yet vicariously wish-fulfilling protagonist, in the tradition of Odysseus and countless other cunning scoundrels with a well-hidden idealistic side. 

Personally, I would go back to Ian Fleming’s source material. Spies like Richard Sorge used womanizing, alcoholism, and reckless driving as cover, because incompetent aristocrats who indulged in those things full time were everywhere, and never seen as having the intellect, discretion, sobriety, or courage to be a spy. Bond should have some modern vices and a similar way of blending in with a crowd seen as mediocre and reliable.

comments.name: Leo A
comments.body:
I would have thought Theo James was a better choice, If you saw him in Guy Ritchies The Gentleman he has all the qualities of a James Bond .

In any case , If you haven't watched seasons 1&2 it's highly recommend.

comments.name: anonymouse
comments.body:
I guess it depends on how brave Amazon wants to be. The Bond franchise is a celebration of toxic masculinity and white male supremacy. Whether there's an audience for that, and how big, depends on how overt they are about it. 

There's a tension between disguising it by toning it down and making it vanilla and fantasy based on the one hand, and being overt while driving the audience away in disgust.

Batman is an antihero but he ultimately fights for justice. What does Bond fight for, really. The preservation of a corrupt sexist, racist system? Think about why Bond can never be black or female.

Ooh here's an idea, what if the next Bond villain was James Bond?

comments.body: One issue was that the US steel industry was built before WWII.  Europe & Asia rebuilt war damaged facilities.  The US never caught up.

comments.name: koyaanisqatsi
comments.body: Americans could not make it work. Our system/our culture simply doesn't work. My Vietnamese TaeKwonDo instructor told me the same story many times. Young kids from East Asia were attentive, obedient, disciplined, and worked hard...for about a year until they become Americanized. Then they didn't listen, were undisciplined and didn't work hard. Frankly, most Americans I knew in the work place were the same way--they just put in their time and went home to whatever. I expect these Japanese imports to behave the same way, especially with Ferchak Americanizing them. I suppose here is some hope that modernizing the plant will make a difference.

comments.name: Simon Harding
comments.body: It's amusing to me that this sort of revitalization is only necessary because business (abetted by both parties and I'll conceived trade agreements) sold out the United States and it's citizens to make an easy buck by off shoring.

comments.name: jeff willaims
comments.body: Hire the workers. Make it as environmentally clean as possible in 2026 and fire up the blast furnaces. Much needed jobs.

comments.name: David
comments.body:
Why are American companies let off the hook for wringing the the last drop of profit out of their critical industries, and everybody turns around and demands the new guy act the opposite?

Why was US Steel allowed to run itself into the ground and Nippon Steel better act right?

It's such a stupid opportunism that we treat ownership changes as the only time to address massive neglect. We do this in housing, too - aluminum wires catching fire and lead paint and pipes are all okay as long as you don't sell the house?

Restoring American manufacturing will require state involvement in critical industries and a serious interest in the details that nobody wants to actually learn.

Three cheers for Nippon so far.

comments.name: Ross Hoch
comments.body: I appreciated the detailed narration of the flip cup anecdote.

comments.name: kallikaknj
comments.body:
U.S. Steel brought about its own demise--and continued degrading the environment--by hanging on to legacy steelmaking processes like the open hearth long after its competitors--domestic and foreign--had moved on.

Readers who have lived within five miles of an "old-school" mill know what I'm talking about: darkness at noon and the smell of sulphur dioxide meant a well-paying job and household security to many.

The rest of the country didn't see a link to these downsides and--in the best American tradition--didn't care.

It is doubly ironic our vanquished foes from WWII are now showing us how to make America great again in one sector we dominated for over a century.

Sadly, just as Trump&Co. welcome Japanese engineering expertise to the Mon Valley, the Administration is aggressively seeking to choke off foreign contributors to federally-funded academic research by withholding visas.

Maybe we should give the Stable Genius a Golden Share in the fruits of that research.

I'm not holding out hope for an epiphany any time soon.

I'm actually kind of amazed that the times mentioned Trump's requirements designed to prevent layoffs and requires billions in investments.  Granted, its presented as a potential negative for Japanese company, but still Trump's intervention resulted in saving and creating jobs.  

You can bet the Democrats will never give him credit for it, but maybe, just maybe, the workers will remember even though the union will do its best to ensure the next president and  congress is Democrat.

comments.name: Jim
comments.body:
The fragility we are seeing in our IT systems is being caused by three things:

1. AI is pushing volumes of data the systems weren't meant to handle, in ways that weren't anticipated.
2. The AI found vulnerabilites are causing us to have to make (on the fly) changes to how systems and applications are built, managed, patched, and that is breaking the paradigm that has evolved over the last 25 years.  
3. There has been a slow decline in the number of IT staff that understand the underlying infrastructure that was built the last 25-30 years.  

It is going to take a big investment in people, process, and tooling to re-engineer how we manage systems, and applications.  

We are operating under the old model and trying to deal with new threats. That is going to keep breaking and breaking with more regularity.

comments.name: Lawrence Lewis
comments.body: What is driving the sudden software failures at hospitals? Can it be the rush to let AI install new software without adequate human review? Just asking?

comments.name: Lawrence Lewis
comments.body: Do we give Ellison a pass on integrity? We know that he is very successful at building mammoth businesses and demanding exemption from any antitrust laws.

comments.name: Momotaro
comments.body: Scary, retired RN BSN do current Healthcare workers remember how to manually take a blood pressure or temperature without technology?

comments.name: AM
comments.body: The attack in France demonstrates how having everything connected to the internet isn’t safe and it’s also unnecessary. Even something like a refrigeration system needs to be isolated from the outside. Patient information needs to be protected, but with ventilators and pharmacies or even lighting systems all connected to the internet, central control of these systems may have opened patients to unanticipated risks.

comments.name: Richard
comments.body:
Good article.  But it brought to light many disturbing issues:

. Far too many data breach and ransomware attacks for far too long.  The hospital industry and government should've stepped up to secure their software long ago.  And years ago hospitals managed just fine using older plain mainframe software without internet connection.

. The Java software was developed by Sun Microsystems years ago.  But now we learn that Oracle bought it out.  We must ask why Oracle, a very large outfit in its own right, was allowed to buy up another large outfit?  Isn't that a violation of anti-trust?  Should Oracle be investigated for anti-trust violations?  It has 21 products just in hospital service.

. We're reminded that refrigeration units of stored blood in France was hacked.

We see that modern mission critical systems--life and death for patients--have grown too complex and unwieldy and are out of control.  For instance, as a patient, I asked for a Tylenol.  It took the nurse a full 15 minutes of typing to give me a pill, despite having a wristband and bottle scanner to record the transaction.  Why was a nurse tied up for so long for something so routine?  That is lousy system design.

. We learned that health records software is at risk for tampering.  That's dangerous for patients.

comments.name: Molly Larson Cook
comments.body:
Hospitals should be rushing to patch patients and not to patching tech glitches or hacks. 

God help us!

comments.name: Diane
comments.body:
“The American Hospital Association said it was not aware of any negative impacts on hospital operations”
— very strange, considering several hospitals have been basically shut down for a while this year. There have been several Iranian hacks this year to smaller hospitals.

articles.title: Hospitals Rush to Patch Java Vulnerabilities

They have.  Warsh should have raised interest rates to combat inflation but can't summon the courage to face down Trump.  That's as partisan as it gets.

comments.name: Rocky

"But the White House replied in late September that Mr. Trump was “skeptical” of that reasoning.".
Trump was skeptical because he himself had already engaged in that kind of similar fraud. But just because Trump did it repeatedly does not mean Governor Cook did.

comments.name: Blandino
comments.body:
How transparent and incompetent are the White House lawyers and their mastermind.  

They wouldn't need to engage in such aggressive, chest-thumping rhetoric if they actually had a leg to stand on.  

It's pathetic, but also enraging that this is a major focus of our current government.  

What's most disgusting is that Trump's attacks on the Federal Reserve are rooted in his desire to drop interest rates, which he believes would create an artificial and temporary feeling of prosperity which he could take credit for.  

The Fed understands that the long-term result would be disastrous inflation, which of course would be blamed on Democrats, but by then Trump will be retired, gloating about how wonderful America was while he was running the show.  

Warsh held them steady last time, but it looks like he's going to have to raise them in December to dampen the gross inflation we're experiencing as a result of the Iran war, matching the English rate raise of a couple of weeks ago.  

The longterm economic fallout from what Trump has done won't be pretty.  

I wish some NYT opinion savant would dilate on this topic.  Where's Paul Krugman now that we really need him?

comments.name: Jim
comments.body:
William O. Scharf, the counsel to the president, said that Ms. Cook’s inability to attend was “unreasonable and disregards the gravity of the allegations against you.”

Where is the gravity?  The Trump Administration is both obvious and ridiculous.  It amazes me that we trust them with so much power and so much of our money.

comments.name: GL
comments.body: Hey Trump should show us his taxes for once and for all!  Then you will see some cheating and fraud the likes of which boggles the mind.

comments.name: John McGlynn
comments.body: What is this? Nothing more than a Soviet show trial from the 1930s. No wonder Trump admires Putin - pure KGB tactics.

comments.name: Jack Toner
comments.body: If she broke the law why hasn't she been indicted? Ah, a small problem with the "evidence"--it won't stand up in a court of law. No problem, convene a special Trumparoo hearing, with no pesky judge to ask impolite questions. So, will this pass muster with the Supremes? There's two who will love it.

articles.title: Fed Governor Cook Won’t Attend White House Hearing Without Changes
articles.summary: Lawyers for Lisa Cook, the Federal Reserve governor President Trump is trying to fire, called the hearing process a “facade.”

comments.name: KP
comments.body: I used to complain that Trump played too much golf. Now I wish that was all he did. imagine if he done nothing. Literally played golf and held rallies. Everyone would be better off

comments.name: betz
comments.body: I don't understand why Trump dislikes Canada.  ??

comments.name: Hillside
comments.body:
A world in disarray needed a stateman, and Mark Carney of Canada was thrust into that role with his speech in Davos January 2026. Carney has been travelling to Europe, Asia, Australia, and Brazil to strengthen Canada's trade and diplomacy with middle power nations. 

Carney the economist saw the significance of middle power countries and the growing trajectory of their economies.

comments.name: John
comments.body: Tariffs are an act of war, and Canada is reacting by alliances with other Countries. It's over with Canada. They have moved to the E.U. and China.  Russia, and North Korea have more in common with the U.S.these days.They even look the same with brigades of troops occupying the Capitals and armored vehicles on the way. Even political appointments live in sequestered military compounds.

comments.name: Trento Cloz
comments.body: Without a Canadian market, FORD and GM will likely go bankrupt. We are their second biggest market by a mile,  and their market share in Canada is dropping like a stone.

comments.name: Fruminous Bear
comments.body:
For our American friends who in this thread are telling us that we'll "regret getting into bed with China," ... here are a few words from Frank Sinatra:

Regrets, we've had a few
But then again, too few to mention
We're doing what we have to do
And seeing it through without exemption
We've planned each chartered course
Each careful step along the by-way
And more, much more than this,
We're doing it our way

comments.name: Appaulled
comments.body: When your friend no longer treats you as a friend, you find new ones. We are well aware of how China is. We are also aware of what the USA is. Both want to take advantage of us. So we move on. We will still trade with Americans but never again will we trust them. We will trade with China as well, but not trust them either. Same with India. That said, trade is nor friendship. Our friends are EU, CPTPP, Francophone and Commonwealth countries.

comments.name: 304th Vet
comments.body: I understand Canada’s consternation with Trump, but getting into bed with China is not the answer, and tney will regret it.

articles.title: Carney and Xi Announce Trade Pact Ahead of Asia Summit
articles.summary: The agreement between Canada and China and the cordial relations on display by their leaders contrast with the current Canada-U.S. relationship.

comments.name: CardinalJedi
comments.body:
The MCU doesn't exist without the work of the King.  

He and Stan were the Lennon and McCartney of graphic art in the late 50s and the entirety of the 60s, including Westerns, and monsters in addition to superheroes.  

Hundreds of artists inside and outside of comics are indebted to Jack's art, passion, creativity, and vision for creator rights.  

Long live the King!

comments.name: michael
comments.body: It is a shame that the article fails to mention the assuredly major impact that being a jew, a member of a demeaned, discriminated against out group, played in his imagination of superheroes.

comments.name: JM
comments.body:
I collected DC, Marvel, Archie Comics, on and on. Like some of the others commenting, I probably had some 400+ comic books - all of which my mom threw out at some point.
Considering what vintage comics are worth today, she threw away thousands of dollars!

comments.name: Thollian
comments.body: Interesting that there is no mention here of Stan Lee. If everyone is a superhero in their own minds, then they need a supervillain nemesis.

comments.name: Sam23
comments.body:
Always big news when a new comic book issue lo came out in my bronx neighborhood. When I couldnt afford the dime the thing cost I would read them in the candy store by the wire rack until the owner tossed me out. I was more a DC comics elementary school kid way back when, but I used to sneak peeks at those romance comics too for a clue - any clue!please!- on how to talk to girls. 

I also loved Classics Illustrated which introduced me to books I would read much later (and found dating tips there too…I can still picture that frame in which Tom Sawyer kissed Becky Thatcher in that cave. For a 10 yo, quite the move). And I read those WW2 comics too, which gave me the briefest glimpse of what my dad, also a Jewish kid from a struggling family who volunteered to go over and kill nazis, may have experienced. 

And like so so many others, MY mom also decided to dump all those cumbersome comics and boxes of baseball cards in my room that could have provided generational wealth for our family. Sigh. It is why I guess Ive become sort of a semi-hoarder of stuff these days. Of course, it wont happen that way. It’s why that Action Comic or that Mantle rookie card is so valuable: it wasnt kept as an investment, more as a fluke. 

Again - also another reminder of the wonderful  impact of Jews on our culture. If you are an anti-semite, maybe you shouldnt act in or profit from or even watch any of the many versions of the characters he and other Jewish kids imagined into being way back when.

comments.name: Dave Kelsen
comments.body: Jack Kirby also drew quite a few DC comics, including "The New Gods," and created characters such as Darkseid The Miracle Man, and many more.

comments.name: Jack Frost
comments.body:
Jack was a very good friend of my mother the late Sylvia Siegel from Brooklyn.  She and Jack's future wife Roselyn were friends from kindergarten throughout their school years and into the war and beyond.  Mom was maid of honor at their wedding. She told of going to the beach with Jack, Roz and friends and then Jack would pick them up and carry them into the waves.  I have pictures of them on the beach.  Many times my mom and dad would travel to meet them at their home in Long Island and I'd enjoy the glider in their backyard.  They'd grill hot dogs for all of us kids and we'd have a nice time.  

I remember much more including when Neil their son was showing me his dad's basement studio and we threw a football into a wall and put a hole in it...Jack wasn't too pleased.  I also remember their daughters including Susan who was a year or two older than me.  Susan told how she sometimes modeled for her dad. And I learned that Roz often did inking for some of Jack's drawings.  

I'm almost 80 now but I still have the pictures my dad took and also that Jack, Roz and my mom took in Brooklyn.  Mom stayed in touch with the Kirby's until they passed away. Roz and mom would often call each other and catch up on where all the kids were and what was new.  Both had 4 children.  When the Kirbys moved to California they still kept in contact with my mom and dad.

The World War II generation was literally the Greatest Generation and we baby boomers were fortunate to be their children.

comments.name: Sycamore
comments.body: Long live Jack Kirby, Magnificent Master of Marvelous Visual Mediums!

articles.title: Birthplace of Many Marvel Superheroes? The Mind of a Lower East Side Boy.
articles.summary: Jack Kirby helped create Iron Man, the Hulk and many other superheroes who went on to great crime-fighting careers and starring roles in movies and TV shows.

comments.name: Tom Koehler
comments.body: It does not bode well for American security practices when a single individual can get himself and what he can conveniently carry, inside of an aircraft like this without apparent help. That he can then wreak such thorough damage and havoc single-handed without being a professional Black Hat, speaks volumes. I have a grudging respect for this man, doing so much with so little, against such a Goliath. His punishment is more for the embarrassment he caused, than the physical damage.

comments.name: Robert
comments.body: The Irish are currently being pressured to join NATO. I hope they resist and become a truly neutral country and stop allowing their airports to be used by foreign militaries

comments.name: Busby
comments.body: 10 years of his precious life behind bars and was it worth it? Nothing was accomplished.

comments.name: No space left
comments.body: Despite our national myth, we are no longer the good guys.  And people hate us.

comments.name: Defeatist
comments.body: My hero.

comments.name: Justin
comments.body: Wow, he really wanted to destroy that thing.  Thinking as a physicist, what are insidious ways to destroy an aircraft -- well, use some gallium-indium eutectic to quickly and irreversibly corrode the aluminum airframe.  But there's no way some vandal could be that clever.  But that's exactly what this guy did!

comments.name: Miss Mew
comments.body:
Like all previous historic Empires, there comes a time when their selfish decisions, negligence, and neglect of the welfare of others in their sphere become so common that citizens of former 'allies' become saboteurs.

This man's intricately planned destruction of a military asset to make it no longer useful is one example of this. The world's people are getting tired of the toxic superpowers that dominate and control others' political systems, resources, technology, survival, etc through economic, political and military bullying.

Expect more of these types of protests. For this is what it truly is.

comments.name: BL
comments.body: I had mice do similar to my pickup truck one time.

articles.title: Irish Man Sabotaged U.S. Military Plane With Ax and Chemicals, Prosecutors Say
articles.summary: Daithi O’Corrain sealed himself inside a National Guard C-130 at Ireland’s Shannon Airport in April for hours, causing so much damage that the aircraft was retired from service, prosecutors said.

comments.name: Wanda Fewka
comments.body: AI is reshaping the world -- and will restructure American political alliances in the process.  New commonalities of concern are emerging, bringing together disparate and often previously hostile demographics. This political restructuring might actually prove to be one of AI's more beneficial effects.

comments.name: Kelly
comments.body: My daughter attends a drama conservatory at an arts college and the students have been pushing for limits on the use of AI. The professors are right there with them. Kids need to take notes and write in class using paper and pencil. They are all keenly aware of the possible damage to the arts. No one is saying no to AI in its entirety and realize the possible benefits, but these creatives know that artistic expression can not just be generated by machine models.

comments.name: Richard
comments.body: Looking back at history: in the calculator era, the US went from banning to accepting over about 20 years. China is trying to do both at once, requiring students to learn to use AI while monitoring it closely in their graded work. Tsinghua went from eight AI-enabled course pilots in autumn 2023 to 451 courses by spring 2026.

comments.name: Ed
comments.body: This is nutty. I’m sponsoring a year-long senior engineering project with a six-person team at a top U.S. college. I want the students using AI to question their assumptions, explore alternatives, and spot gaps in their reasoning. If they skip that step, I may get a weaker design/prototype, and they miss a chance to learn how to use a valuable engineering tool. I’ve asked them to run their deliverables through AI for feedback before they send them to me. It’s a hot topic on campus. Those wanting AI are winning the debate.

comments.name: winds
comments.body: A friend was telling me that AI can do everything a Lawyer can do. He said we wont even need lawyers in the future, That may be true but Im sure you will still pay for the services. AI will charge just as much as a lawyer. Have you heard of surveillance pricing? Currently People are already paying higher interest because of the boom in data centers not to mention the damage to environment. All so a few guys like Musk can control the world. Not the world i want to live in

comments.name: Anonymous
comments.body: Were I a college student during this time, I would apply a watermark to any assignment that I hand in, attesting to my non-use of AI. "This work was produced without AI technology." Something to that effect. To formally state, for the record, that I am fully committed to the learning process. Whether or not my professor gives me extra credit for not letting a computer do my work for me is beside the point.

comments.name: Michael
comments.body:
I don't understand why college administrators aren't fighting to be the university that most emphatically rejects the use of AI.

If one of our universities announced that they are banning all uses of AI in order to focus on their true mission of developing and nurturing critical thinking, overnight, this school would become the most interesting and talked about university in our country!

 It would instantly separate this university from the rest of the pack, and make it extremely desirable to a certain type of highly motivated, thoughtful, and mature student. The exact type of student that universities are competing for.

It's a no brainer!

comments.name: Peter T
comments.body: I'm a university professor who constantly deals with the drawbacks of AI. Still, I don't think a blanket ban or refusal to use AI entirely is the way forward. There are plenty of legitimate uses for it and employers will increasingly expect graduates to use it in their work. Instead, we need to figure out and provide clearer guidance on when it is and isn't appropriate to use AI. For starters, professors should stop assigning any work or conducting assessments that can be done using AI, and professors should not be allowed to use AI for grading.

articles.title: The Anti-A.I. Campus Movement Is Growing
articles.summary: Some students are refusing to use A.I., and others are starting petitions to limit it across entire campuses. Colleges have taken notice.

comments.name: Nest Dricely
comments.body: Besides unnecessarily over-complicating (and under-explaining) why folks are attracted to authority figures, the article proposes measures which amount to little more than brainwashing children, in public schools, no less. Time and again, when any level of government tries to shape what children believe, families resist – through the courts, at the ballot box, and sometimes even violently. It’s one thing to propose a common value, as a normative goal, in a pluralistic society, and another to assume that force-feeding it to American children is a plausible way to attain it.

comments.name: Hazlit
comments.body:
One of the fundamental errors of this piece and others like it is the presumption that right wing people are hierarchical and left wing people are not, or at least are less so. 

Yet this assumption conceals a paradox. To value equality over inequality is itself a hierarchy. To value goodness over cruelty is a hierarchy. To choose between A and B, and ultimately A over B is necessarily to make a hierarchy. Once one value is placed over another it is effectively a hierarchy.

comments.name: Phrancis
comments.body: Given the human struggle for survival over thousands of years, it seems logical that core beliefs about dangers, hierarchy, or loyalty to strong leaders would be common and perhaps even have a genetic disposition. There's a comforting certainty in these concrete beliefs. I can't help but notice how conservatives want to see the world in absolutist binary terms: good and bad, left and right, male and female, or black and white, where the truth is often shades of grey. Ambiguity and open-mindedness is a danger to them.

comments.name: Dr. Josie
comments.body: The biggest impact for me about how I viewed the world was travel as a student on Semester at Sea. Not only was I exposed to many different cultures and ways of being, but I also came to understand that these 'other' people had a right to do so. Travel can be mind expanding and a real portal into the lives of others. I'm so grateful I had that experience!

comments.name: Lawrence Lewis
comments.body: Has the USA gone past the recovery point of Hobbesism to save our democratic republic even with the last election? We will need at least a decade to repair the damage done to our federal government by DOGE alone. The psychological damage to citizens will take generations. One election is just the beginning. We must not allow the current idea of lazie-faire government to regain it's near absolute control.

comments.name: MDW
comments.body: Considering just this article, primal theory should at some point (maybe it already has) address the pull of the alternative theory of cognitive identitarianism. The first covert thought of that dynamism is "X is what I want to be and the attributes of X make me feel strong and secure. The second is closed-minded commitment of an ongoing nature: "X has my allegiance now and forever."

comments.name: Robert
comments.body:
Isn't this just another phrasing of a joke I learned when I was living in Communist Romania in the late 1980s/early 90s? A farmer is standing in the total ruins of his natural disaster ravaged farm. God speaks to him, telling him that since he has suffered so much, he will be granted his heart's desire. The farmer looks over to his neighbors untouched farm and says, "Make the same things happen to him." I have since heard many versions of that joke from all over the world.

The point being there is a strong strand of cruelty that has seems to go hand-in-hand with authoritarian-oriented conservatism. A willingness to live in misery as long as everyone else is forced to live in the same misery.

I am not sure these folks have some hierarchical list of importance as much as they simply fear everything, and in their fear, feel compelled to lash out. It's the fear that is the problem; not their ever-shifting list of targets they want punished.

comments.name: Dennis Schumacher
comments.body:
Most of this discussion does not incorporate where the personal ego and its overwhelming fear of not existing.   Out of this primal force all the other fears spring such as physical well-being and the emotional fear of not existing. No wonder many individuals can be deceived about the false safety of authoritarian leaders. 
Dennis Schumacher

articles.title: Voters Are Punishing Autocrats. But Many Still Embrace Them. Why?
articles.summary: An emerging field of psychology suggests that it’s probably not what you think — and that there might be reason for optimism.

comments.name: NoSurprise
comments.body: Advanced technology is a matter of national security, and we must undoubtedly guard it. At the same time, we have to credit and respect the people making it happen.

comments.name: Eddie B.
comments.body:
"Will a Spy Scandal, Trade Friction and a Surprise Guest Ruin Xi’s Big Moment?"

I don't see why Xi would allow his "big moment" to be ruined. He has all the tools - or to use Mr. Trump's lingo "all the cards" - he needs to control the situation. He can:

1. Completly ignore the "spy scandal". And if it was raised by others, Xi can always treat it as a Taiwan-US problem, using the fact that Mr. Huang has Taiwan citizenship. He can also bring up the fact that Huang Le (Alice Huang) is a Hong Kong resident;

2. Signal he would resort to cutting off the US from key rare earth minerals once again, if the US decided to increase "trade frictions" with China; and,

3. North Korea is heavily dependent on China. Xi can let Kim Jong Un to know he doesn't want him to come to Shenzhen. That will be the end of it.

comments.name: Grunt
comments.body: There is no there there with the fact free spy allegations. Jensen Huang was not privy to any classified information, and he would be the wrong person from whom to steal chip designs—a CEO carries nothing of substance and it’s not like he can verbally divulge useful trade secrets on chip design. Even if China gets its hands on NVidia’s actual latest chip design, it can’t manufacture them—only one company in the world can:  TSMC. From all accounts, she was seemingly just a smuggler for China’s internet giants, like Alibaba and Tencent, but surely the MSS would be aware of her actions. In any event, 600,000 H200 chips are sitting in Hong Kong, barred by China from entering even though they were legally purchased. China since 2025 had ordered all of their AI companies to use Huawei chips, despite their being slower and less energy efficient. China would rather use 4x the energy to achieve AI parity through optical clustering of their Huawei chips than kowtow to US restrictions. All this nonsense about spying is just pure nonsensical politics that has destroyed $2T of US wealth in weeks.

comments.name: Juan
comments.body: I’m against almost every foreign policy decision that this administration makes, but I must say Trumps ability to connect on a personal level does make the world seem like a slightly safer place.  Xi and Putin are what they are, but culturally how you treat them in public I think matters, especially to Xi. I feel it’s the right move to be “friendly”, while playing hardball behind the scenes.

comments.name: Kurt
comments.body: I can’t help imagining how the conversation in Shenzhen will go, if the Nvidia spy subject comes up at all. Will President Xi confess: “Yes, she was ours, and a very good one. Thanks to her, we have thousands of your most advanced chips to build systems designed to defeat the very country that sold them to us”? Of course not. He will say he has never heard of her, and that China does not spy on other nations. Everybody knows that. And I fear our President will simply nod along.

comments.name: Runaway
comments.body: Greeting Trump at the airport was simply flattery. It will work.

comments.name: ksanger
comments.body: We the People should ruin Xi's big moment. When my company sent me to China to work with them to build machines for us I complained loudly. But I still went in order to preserve my pension and retire as quickly as I could. In the interim my company went bankrupt. The Chinese went on without us. While we were there they showed us a competitive machine that they had just finished copying.  There was the quiet minder sitting in on every meeting.  Her only role was to report back to Beijing on all of our technology that we were discussing. Not to mention that our Chinese businessman had a silent partner. You want to bet that the Chinese government was the silent partner?  Trump has tried and failed to stop this. He's absolutely the wrong person to do so. He's too easy to manipulate and most likely bribeable. He is absolutely correct that China is a threat to the United States. We are addicted to their inexpensive products. Our Companies are extremely embedded in China and no longer should be considered American. They have a stake and investment overseas.  Our Companies have also corrupted the Republican Party and have a huge influence in our elections.  Just think if we all just stopped, delayed, or just minimized our next Chinese purchase.  We have power.  Honest leadership could bring it out of us. The United States is unbeatable when we are united and act together. Buy Chinese products. China buys Iran and Russian Oil. We indirectly help kill Ukrainians and sponsor Iran.

comments.name: jhar
comments.body:
Xi is just being Xi -- and Trump has been working for him by helping China surreptitiously obtain proprietary American technology through his pal Huang at Nvidia. 

Xi's position hasn't changed. He holds all the cards. And Trump is the face on his Joker.

articles.title: Will a Spy Scandal, Trade Friction and a Surprise Guest Ruin Xi’s Big Moment?
articles.summary: The leader wants the APEC summit to showcase China’s strengths, but he faces export worries and an unpredictable Trump, who has floated meeting Kim Jong-un.

comments.name: Jeff
comments.body: There is something very satisfying about building anything with rocks.  On our Connecticut property all you need to do is dig a bit and you'll soon have boulders and rocks of all sizes. I've been using them to build stack stone landscaping walls which manage the slope of our yard.  One project leads to another with more stone, a shed, steps to our fire pit, and a play area for grandchildren. These are all called "15 minute projects" in jest because they require considerable time and effort.  Congrats on completing projects ....eventually!

comments.name: B.A. Shipley
comments.body: Let me first say how much I admire the dream and the work - it looks beautiful. I'm not an architect or engineer, and I ask this question without malice, but what about the stone work is "structural"? It's a veneer - albeit a rather thick / deep one, but it's not actually tied into the existing structural system, is it? I'd appreciate some clarity on this. Thanks.

comments.name: Eric
comments.body: The interface between the original siding and the new stonework could be a real problem point for moisture.  I am sure they know what they are doing, but I am curious HOW they are addressing this.

comments.name: Kathy Watson
comments.body: I would really love to hear how the stone has changed the environment inside the house. I imagine it stays cooler in summer, and perhaps retains heat better in winter?

comments.name: Mark Farr
comments.body: That stone and brick-work: so deeply beautiful. Like coming across a Rembrandt in a gallery full of Thomas Kinkade's.

comments.name: BOBBY BEDFORD
comments.body: not sure this is a good idea ... an 18" old stone barrier  as a facade  on a stick-built modern dwelling... others have mentioned old stone has 1/10th insulation value modern materials, what about  ground shifts, the weight of the stone facade might cause ground compression or sink...how do you get " behind the facade " to deal with moisture-structural problems on the  interface ?

comments.name: Patricia
comments.body: Great story.   Would love to see photos of the "tree house".

comments.name: Raymond Rice
comments.body: This project reminds me of what Martijn Doolaard has been doing in the Italian alps: the patient building of stone walls by hand. I've been watching his progress for years by tuning into his eponymous YouTube channel.  Few thought he would finish the project, but he did. A stone wall is not built in a day, but eventually it comes together. I appreciated the patience and time that goes into something like this.

articles.title: Transforming a House Upstate, Stone by Stone
articles.summary: Can an architect turn his family’s new build into a dwelling that looks centuries-old? He’s getting there.

comments.name: Jim D
comments.body: This article made many important points, especially that electrification is a "prerequisite", that is to say, a necessary condition, for transitioning to clean energy.  However, "But even in countries that power their grids with fossil fuels, electric machines use less energy than those that burn coal, oil and gas," is too sweeping.  That is not always the case for the system consisting of the generation unit, the transmission lines, and the final use by any means.  It depends critically on how efficient the generation and transmission is.  Older coal fired plants are often so wasteful of energy, that even though the electric motors they energize are extremely efficient, the overall energy consumption is worse than direct use of a cleaner fossil fuel like natural gas in a heat engine.  Of course, it is still urgent that countries, particularly the US, make China-scale efforts to electrify, and to do so in technically sound ways.

comments.name: Gary C
comments.body: Investing in smart grid infrastructure would allow dial output up or down nuclear power sources, regional wind and solar surpluses along with battery storage to be efficiently moved around.  We’re a large modern country with many options that aren’t beholden to the petroleum or coal industries.  They have and will continue to lobby against that future.  That worked well with Trump, but we just rejected that corruption.

comments.name: MadAsHell
comments.body: I've fully electrified my home and my transportation. As a result I avoid over $9,000 annually that I would be paying for fossil fuel energy had I not electrified.  Electrifyng  is a better alternative.

articles.title: There’s a New Push at Climate Talks: Wire the World for Electricity
articles.summary: With war squeezing global oil and gas supplies, leaders at COP31 are backing a plan that would mirror China’s rapid grid expansion.

comments.name: Dave
comments.body: Parking enforcement is quick to tow. Luckily, when I parked at what seemed to be a totally okay spot, I was warned to park on the other side of the street. As we returned from our hike, a bewildered man was standing there wondering where his car had gone.

comments.name: Dan
comments.body: I have a property on a street that has become a tick tock sensation (millions of views) due to views of Downtown L A. It has taken a few years for the city of L A to do anything about it. However there is little they can do. It's terrible how unmannered the young adults are on our street. Trash, parties in the street, car races, drugs etc. So I can assure you it's much worse than the Hollywood Sign neighborhood. Note, I bought the property before this became a social media destination. It's cheap thrills for the youth.

comments.name: Linda
comments.body: Mr. Bircher mentioned the answer to the problem. Take the sign down. Having it up for a hundred years is long enough. The heyday of Hollywood has passed, anyway. Most movies aren't even made there anymore. Film production has moved out of California to other states like Georgia and New Mexico that offer more attractive tax incentives. Other countries like Canada and the UK are also used more frequently. Get rid of the sign and put it in the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures in LA.

comments.name: Chaz
comments.body: The sign is quite visible from many vantage points that don’t involve creating fire and traffic hazards and pollution. Not to mention trespass as evidenced by the photo of a woman standing on someone else’s property. Access should be severely limited here. Sure the sign has been up for 100 years or so, but Instagram has only been around for 15 or so. I feel very bad for anyone who lives up there. It is ruining their quality of life.

comments.name: Gizendorder
comments.body: Just because the sign has always been there doesn't mean that it was always a problem.  In this day and age of tourism on steroids and seemingly everyone feeling like they have to have their selfie at every site it's quite a different thing than it was even a couple of decades ago.  How many folks in less renown, rural areas have found themselves dealing with the same sort of problems because their once bucolic site suddenly caught the attention of the on line public?  it's no different than the people in certain cities in Europe who have decided that the tourism they once welcomed is now ruining their lives.  It's all just too much.

comments.name: stephan morrow
comments.body:
I spent the 90's in L.A. (brought out there by being in Mailer's 'Tough Guys Don't Dance' ) but where I ended up putting together an 'artists residency' (23 writers, actors, directors & just what you would have to call L.A. jetsam and flotsam ) on Wilton/Franklin. I would run up Beechwood Cyn to the Sunset Ranch and I remember one time there was a film or commercial being shot and the director was in awe that someone was running up that steep road. For awhile I had a girlfriend who would ride horses from there and it got to where they would just give me a horse and I would go alone into the hills and past the Sign. Sunset Ranch was a kick, 'course many things were shot there. But that road was deserted. Just a steep, dusty blacktop on a California hillside. No one but me running up it - and sometimes my girl. Can't believe what I'm seeing: a traffic jam there ?? So strange since the sign has been there for decades. So what's happened in the last 25 yrs? I lost my heart up there. Is it cursed? Had a dream of assuaging the pain by seeking some counseling from Shelly Winters RIP (I knew her well) who was nestled among the O and LL dispensing advice. The vibe going down to the flats made people do bad things as they foamed at the mouth from the disease of ambition. (everyone knew they were 3 phone calls away from being a household name). Made them nuts. (never found out what happened to her - & didn't want to). Just a bad job. 
Artistic Director
The Great American Play Series

comments.name: Lifelong California Resident
comments.body:
I grew up in Los Angeles and now live in Sacramento. I’ve watched California grow tremendously, and the streets near landmarks like the Hollywood sign were built long before they had to handle this much traffic and sightseeing. I understand why residents want the city to step in. Whatever the income of a neighborhood, the people who live there deserve to be heard and to enjoy some peace at home.

This is exactly why we elect city council members. We count on them to listen to residents and help solve problems like this. I may be missing some of what’s been done, but from where I sit, it’s hard to see what the council member representing the area has done to address these concerns. I’d welcome hearing what steps they’ve taken and what they plan to do next.

The city should enforce the rules already on the books and put together a practical plan for traffic, parking, and vendors. People should be able to visit the Hollywood sign, and neighbors should be able to get home and enjoy their neighborhood in peace.

articles.title: Fans Flock to This Famous Sign. Neighbors Say, Get Off My Road.

I've lived in Thailand for 8 years, during which Thailand's ties to China have increased noticeably. Thailand sells fruits, rice and other food products to China, and while the trade deficit is real, it's tolerable. This year 9 million Chinese tourists will visit Thailand. 

When I buy food products online, American products are double the price of foods from other countries. I've discovered a myriad of foods from around the world that rival the quality of US food products and at half the price. Trump's Tariffs keep American goods off of Thai shelves. 

Thai people don't care a whit about MAGA or Republicans or Democrats, but they do care about being treated unfairly by an ignorant US President whose understanding of economics is at a junior high school level. Thais are more than happy to buy Chinese goods whose quality is good and prices affordable. BYD cars are everywhere in Thailand, which has set a goal of 50% EV by 2030, a goal the US hasn't even considered under "oily" Trump.

comments.name: Chen Yu
comments.body: I run a major biotech investment firm and this article skews way too much toward the negative on the biotech relationship with China.  It ignores all of the incredible benefits. One, we start many companies in the US based on China sourced technology.   That creates thousands of jobs in the US that otherwise would not have been created.   Two, unlike in tech where we are worried about high tech leaking to a peer competitor, this is the reverse.  We are getting their novel technology.  Three, if we ban our ability to invest in Chinese companies, we can't see all the competition and that stops us from even investing in US co's because of risk.   It's important to remember we're developing drugs for patients--raising the cost or making it more difficult also increases ultimate drug pricing.  There is no advantage to creating walls here.

comments.name: Osip
comments.body:
Just another example of how money and markets debases and corrupts something that serves a higher function.  

At its best science is about trust and cooperation for the benefit of everyone.  It’s a public good.  Nonrivalrous and nonexcludable.  

This article is about the problems associated with trying exclude the nonexcludable through manmade rules.  How do you profit from the public good?

But, of course someone needs to pay for science.  For years the American people have been allocating a portion of their massive collective surplus to pay for it and private investors put in their own money to bring it to market.

What this is really about is the last part.  And for a group of people who taut the efficiencies of markets and worship competition like a god you do put up quite the hissy fit when you find yourself being outcompeted.  Now you are so angry you are going to just give them the silent treatment.

I don’t understand.  If you just want to make money why didn’t you go into finance?

comments.body: Sometimes it's lost on folks but here it is, plain and true: Binghamton/Tri-Cities, and the whole southern tier of NY going out to Elmira/Corning were at one time among the most prosperous communities anywhere in the country.  The American middle-class was rooted in cities like these.  Endicott-Johnson, IBM, Corning Glass, and a whole massive ecosystem of other companies and institutions.  Between 1945 and 1985 the United States had created, by choice and broad policy, a wonder of the world: the most wide-spread middle-class the world had ever known.  Of course, that is all gone now.  The choices made that killed places like this constitute a crime of the highest magnitude in my book.  A crime that is on-going.  Maybe the carousels can remind us of something that was taken, a crime underway, and maybe cause us to begin the hard work of understanding that and demanding something different.

I hope these kids’ treasures are preserved for future generations. They are a cornerstone in Binghamton’s reputation as a great place to raise children.

comments.name: Upmacman
comments.body: When Spielberg was shooting "Jurassic Park" he was intending to use stop motion animation to add motion to the dinasours. This requires shooting a frame and then moving the model in increments. This technique which is incredibly time consuming had been used from the begining of cinema and in clasics such as "King Kong". The animation crew had already started when someone reminded him that there were severel computer guys who were using a new process that was better and quicker. When Spielberg saw the test footage he went back to the stop motion crew and announced that he was going to use computer graphics  and they could learn to use it or move on. The AI use in the production of special effects has already arrived and will certainly replace the the current techniques for rotoscoping, just as stop motion animation was replaced by CG. Better-Quicker-Cheaper usually prevails in all profit-driven industries.
