comments.body: One thing for sure, that dude has lot of cool coats.

articles.title: Nvidia Has No Plans to Bring Back Jensen Huang
articles.summary: As the former chief executive and his allies lobbied for his return, the company’s chair said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as C.E.O.”

comments.name: Garen Wintemute
comments.body: On that Council on Criminal Justice summit: it's worth noting that the participants ranked expanded community violence intervention (CVI) efforts right behind the easing of pandemic-related restrictions. There's a good deal of evidence supporting the participants' decision. Cities can undertake CVI efforts with some expectation of success.

comments.name: Frederic Cohen
comments.body: For many years the United States has incarcerated a larger percentage of its population than almost every other advanced country. During that time we have become more aware of the harms mass incarceration does, sometimes unnecessarily, to individuals, families and communities. But is it also possible that, as intended, it has incapacitated enough criminals to have a positive effect on crime rates? I am not defending mass incarceration but its relatrionship to crime rates does seem to call for more study as well as caution if policies are changed to reduce prison populations.

comments.name: M.
comments.body: I’m sure there has been some reduction in some crime. However, it’s hard to take claims of crime’s reduction seriously when it is also the case that cities have dramatically curtailed enforcement.

comments.name: Jon
comments.body:
I'll believe claims, but I would love to see the original data, especially Matt Ashby's.

I also wonder how the European cities are defined, and which areas are included in the crime statistics. Americans may feel that European cities are safer if they never leave the central tourist zones, while the data could include those cities' suburban areas.

comments.name: Mark
comments.body: 2021 is a bad year for comparison.  I’d rather see a comparison to 2019.  Pandemic made cities crazy - but it was a blip as with so much of that time.  Also feels like cities are richer now - at least NYC - forcing out the poor.

comments.name: CH
comments.body:
The usual Democratic/left story about crime. 
In their world, it is always going down and we always needs fewer police. 
But crime is an enormous problem here in Seattle, both for small businesses and residential neighborhoods, especially in certain places. 
Homelessness likewise. 
Yes, there are successes in some places like NYC.
But if the left thinks it can forget about crime and public safety, think again.

comments.name: John Murphy
comments.body: It’s the prevalence of cameras everywhere. Bad guys are getting caught, convicted and doing time due to the incontrovertible evidence provided by the everywhere videographers in cars, doorbells, and traffic systems. Less bad guys equals less killings and crime overall. Plus, the belief that with so many guns in private hands that everyone and every household is armed, fewer bad guys are willing to take the risks involved in criminal behavior. The only question that leaves is what are the bad guys doing for money and where are they doing it?

comments.name: AJ
comments.body: I think a lot of it boils down to gentrification and the fact that many cities are attractive and growing again, especially for young people, but even for some older people. Increased population, with more people on the street, deters crime. I suspect this is why crime rose during covid. People were idle, not going out as much, so some idle people took advantage of the situation. In some cities, the poor have been pushed out of certain neighborhoods once known for crime, so impoverished areas now lie in some of the aging inner ring suburbs - similar to some European cities like Paris. I'm not suggesting that gentrification is a good thing, but I've seen inner city neighborhoods be completely transformed due to investment and one upside might be reduced crime. Then again, while I remember driving through cities with hollowed out neighborhoods where crime was rampant in the 80s and 90s, I don't remember seeing unhoused encampments under bridges and in parks or open spaces and such back then.

articles.title: American Cities May Never Have Been Safer. We Don’t Know Why.
articles.summary: Urban crime rates are near record lows.

comments.name: David Roy
comments.body:
What doesn't make any sense to me is how people use science to check their weather everyday, rely on the science of GPS to travel, go to the doctor and get healthcare based on science, and learn about the formation of our universe based on science.

We do all of this without thinking once about it, trust it, and, mostly, enjoy the benefits of science.

Climate change, which science has shown is not a theory, is refuted by an entire swarth of society that should know better.  Profits over survival seems like a fairly wrong-headed strategy.

And amazing cognitive dissonance.

And which threatens our entire civilization.

Fascinating, in a tragic and morbid sort of way.

comments.name: Bob Tonnor
comments.body: “The climate crisis has not gone away, in fact it’s worsened,” said Chris Bowen, minister for climate change and energy for Australia, who is leading the negotiations in Turkey. “Countries around the world are dealing with natural disasters which are no longer natural, and dealing with impacts they never thought they would have to deal with.”  And they just pushed through a load more coal mine and gas drilling approvals.

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
The Earth is like a giant iron ball. It takes a lot of pushing to get it to roll.

Well, we’ve been pushing hard for 100 years and it’s starting to roll. 

Before long we’ll be begging it to stop.

comments.name: Heather
comments.body: Was walking to an appointment in Clinton Hill Brooklyn this morning and noted rose bushes covered in newly budding flowers. It is November 18th! The roses normally bloom in June!

comments.name: Paulette Altmaier
comments.body: The UN talks where people jetted in from all over the world to bemoan emissions? Many on private jets?

comments.name: R
comments.body: Add to the shocking signs of climate change - 2 waterspouts appeared in the SF Bay a couple of days ago, and one of the drivers was unusually warm bay waters. I have lived here off and on my entire life and never heard of a water spout on the bay.

comments.name: Ingrid Akerblom
comments.body: And this is before all the new gas-fired power plants spin up for datacenters across the US. Hard to have hope.

comments.name: Robert D
comments.body: Since when have the governments of the world act with any urgency with regard to climate change? They’re very good at looking concerned and making useless statements about doing something at some point in the future, maybe. They’re really good at making special pleadings as to why we can’t do something right now and why their country needs exemptions from doing anything.

articles.title: ‘Shocking’ Signs of Climate Change Add Urgency to Latest U.N. Talks
articles.summary: From the Arctic to the tropics, unusual weather and extreme heat is sparking worry about how quickly humans are reshaping the Earth’s natural processes.

comments.name: Shiloh
comments.location: Glenbard West HS Glen Ellyn, IL
comments.body: No, never. Roller coasters are meant to produce a thrill, they cause adventure seeking. Although some coasters have become unsafe, that's no reason to rule out building more. I am a huge fan of roller coasters and I don’t think we should stop building and challenging the metal to its greatest extent. That’s where all the fun is. Roller coasters aren’t just about being scared, it’s about the movement. The twists and turns, the loops, the feeling that you’re about to fly out of the seat and you should hold on for dear life. It’s about people being about to say they have finally been on a roller coaster with a loop-de-loop. Building up to the scarier rides at the amusement park is what my summer was always about. Will I finally ride it? The thrill of hearing a new coaster is coming has me jumping up and down. Pushing the limits doesn’t always result in injury. Yes there are some cases, but not all coasters cause that.

comments.name: Tyler
comments.body: In my opinion I don’t mind roller coasters all that much but some I find to be scary/extreme. Overall yes, I agree roller coasters have become extreme. I think there are roller coasters that have bad safety precautions. I agree roller coasters have become extreme because I have heard on the news that there have been many cases in which people have died/ been severely injured on a roller coaster because of how extreme they have gotten. But, it may not be just because they are so extreme and scary, it might be the safety precautions that the workers are supposed to help with the riders, that is a big factor. I still stand with the fact that they have gotten too extreme though.

comments.name: Colin Dougherty
comments.body: Roller coasters aren’t for me, but I understand why people love them. However, this is a huge issue. Safety needs to come first. As much fun as it is fun to get that thrill, it can’t come at the expense of peoples’ safety. Moreover, it’s not just simply unsafe but potentially lethal. People have been dying, and that’s way more of a problem. More guidelines need to be put in place to prevent any danger, and keep those roller coaster riders safe.

comments.name: Purnima Cha
comments.body: I usually do not enjoy roller coasters due to my acrophobia. However, when I go to amusement parks, I have often noticed that though many of my friends enjoy the roller coaster (perhaps to an unhealthy amount), it also seems very detrimental to our health. The possibility of whiplash from the rollercoaster's jerking, jolting movement also worries me tremendously. Therefore, I would say that roller coasters definately should have some sort of safety feature. I believe that one good example is in Korea, where most rollercoasters have a huge metal belt that all riders must use or else the rollercoaster will not function properly. I hope that other rollercoaster companies will also try adapting their rollercoasters to include these features in their rides to ensure both safety and amusement for the riders who just want to have fun at amusement parks.

comments.name: Amber
comments.body: I think roller coasters are exciting, but safety should always come first. Some people enjoy extreme rides, but they can also be dangerous. I believe amusement parks should focus more on safety instead of making rides faster and scarier. Having fun is important, but protecting people’s lives is more important.

comments.name: Joshua Gerecht
comments.body: I think if they make changes they need to worry about safety a bit more. I also think that the people and companies who are creating these roller coasters are worrying too much about the actual fun and should focus on that and safety. In conclusion I think some rides are too extreme which is fine if they were more safe. However a lot of them aren't if they were to make roller coasters just a bit safer I would have a different opinion though.

comments.name: ML
comments.body:
20 years ago, I went to Knotts Berry Farm on a day that was so empty, we had to wait for other patrons before they would start the ride.  None as extreme as today, nor even the Kumba I rode at Busch Gardens.  So, I was able to ride as many roller coaster that day as in all my previous experience.

At 3pm, my head was spinning badly.  I had to lie down on a bench for a full hour to recover.

Roller coasters can be dangerous.  Today, I wouldn't attempt a kiddie roller coaster because of a bad lumbar spine.

comments.name: Yelena
comments.body: Roller Coasters have always been a huge thing in my life, especially the high speed ones. Falcon's Flight in Six Flags, New Jersey, was a joy to go on. I had to beg my friend to go on with me since they weren't a big fan of roller coasters. The suspense before the big drop was terrifying and fun at the same time, as you go flying down you can feel the blood rushing up your head. My friend who’s deathly afraid of roller coasters had actually changed their mind after a few tries with Falcon's Flight. I feel like people need to get used to the adrenaline and have to trust themselves with the engineers of the roller coasters.

articles.title: Have Roller Coasters Become Too Extreme?
articles.summary: After a man died and others were injured from roller coasters this year, safety has become a concern again. Should ride manufacturers keep pushing the limits?

comments.name: Wim Roffel
comments.body:
US foreign policy since World War II has been to foment hostility between Russia and Europe. If Europe and Russia unite they wouldn't need the US and the US would lose its influence was the thinking.

But with the rise of China this line of thinking no longer works. It drives Russia in the arms of China and that is not in the interest of the US. 

So we see now a hesitant change in US foreign policy. Not everyone has gotten the memo and there is still quite some resistance. But just like Trump's tariffs it is a policy that is likely to survive when Trump is replaced by a Democrat. 

There is also the problem for the US how to keep its influence once Europe and Russia are no longer enemies. At the moment the most visible effort is a power grab within NATO.

comments.name: Vasyl Petrovich Holoborodko
comments.body:
To understand what Russia’s goals are look at how it’s carrying out the war. War crimes have become so ordinary the past five years that we barely register the brazen and grotesque destruction of civilian infrastructure needed for basic survival. Tens of thousands of Ukrainian children have been abducted to be raised as Russians and militarized to fight in future expansionist wars. Millions of Ukrainians have fled the country with millions more internally displaced. This is a genocide. And not the first that Russia has committed against Ukraine (and others) in its long imperial history.

Further, Putin is willing to sacrifice over a million of his own population to destroy Ukraine. He openly pines for an era when Russia killed millions to gain territory and achieve “greatness.” How on earth do you negotiate with such a madman and why would you expect him to stop?

comments.name: Peter
comments.body: Trump is handling Putin either like a fool, or like he's soley interested putting up trump themed towers across Russia.

comments.name: David
comments.body: Can only imagine how gleeful and thankful Putin is the United States elected a clueless buffoon and a Congress beholden to him. He must wake up every day wondering if it is a dream.

comments.name: john fiva
comments.body:
Trump is pathetic with these people he thinks are his friends.
Just a fool really but in two months or so he won't matter and of course they know it. They are dictators but he is not, fortunately!

comments.name: Seal Team Sith
comments.body: Gee, you did not need the CIA, NSA and a Ph.D. to figure that one out.  One thing will end the Ukraine War:  Putin being gone (from power or dead).

comments.name: Anthony
comments.body: Trump. Always believes Putin, not our Intelligence. Besides the three are agreeing that each get what, each believe is theirs. USA - Venezuela, Panama canal, Canada...Russian Ukraine. China -Taiwan. Then there is be peace. Trump will ask for a noble prize

comments.name: RonRich
comments.body: Are we supposed to believe that not talking is better than talking?

articles.title: Putin Will Continue Ukraine War Despite Plans to Meet Trump, Intelligence Says
articles.byline: Edward Wong, Julian E. Barnes and Jeanna Smialek
articles.summary: President Trump plans to discuss Ukraine with the leaders of Russia and China. He has halted some sanctions on Russia and announced that the United States will buy Russian diesel.

comments.name: Jeff
comments.body: Great article.  Visited Madrid a few years ago.  Wonderful, very alive city.  Markets were a real adventure and treat.  Word of caution- lots of pickpockets and thievery.  Be vey careful with your wallet and bags.

comments.name: LH
comments.body: As others have said, same is true all over. That being said, if you make it to Málaga, be sure to eat at the Mercado Carmen's cafe. Best fried baby squid on the planet. This mercado is near the train station - be sure to get to the cafe at 1:30 and you'll get a table. Later than that you could be out of luck.

comments.name: Mx
comments.body: Reminds me of the time I lived in Seattle. On my way home from work, I would get off the bus in front of the Pike Place Market. Whatever looked good, I would buy to make dinner with. Sometimes I took a detour to grab a snack or pop in one of the shops to see if there was anything that caught my eye.  One time I snagged a pair of John Fluvog shoes on deep discount.

comments.name: Vin
comments.body: Mercado's are one of the first places to visit as a traveler. It's a first hand look at what locals are enjoying. I found visiting Madrid, no different than when I visited other European cities Mercado's . Even traveling in Brazil, where restaurants can be somewhat far and few between, Mercado's are everywhere too be enjoyed.

comments.name: Chase
comments.body:
Looking at the photos, beautiful as they are, one sees few locals apart from shoppers at the fruit stand. And the prices posted here? Definitely out of reach of many locals. 

Markets throughout Europe are a wonderful experience. It's just a shame to see so many reoriented toward the tourist trade.

comments.name: Luna
comments.body: Have a breakfast at Museo del Jamón... It's a chain and the food is good BUT the breakfast is the real deal: ham (bacon), eggs, toast and coffee all enough for two. Sit at the counter. There is one across the street up from the Prado.

comments.name: Frida's Mom
comments.body: Thank you for this delightful article. l have traveled all over the Planet thanks to my job as a science journalist. I have never visited Madrid but after reading this piece, I am inspired to move Madrid to the top of my list of cities to visit this year.

comments.name: Frutas Selectas
comments.body: With the exception of La Boqueria, the markets in Barcelona are soulless. Something about the newer markets feel cookie cutter and ordinary. The market in Sant Antoni is depressing. I avoid markets like the plague now whereas when I first moved here I actively sought out the older markets that have now been torn down and replaced with sterile generic newer versions. What's more the stalls are underwhelming: prices are higher and there's little to justify shopping in markets when you can buy better goods elsewhere. I believe in their concept but just like the former bullring, Las Arenas, was converted into a mall that could be in Des Moines, if I were the alcalde of Barcelona, Las Arenas would be the premier concert venue in Europe instead of Palau Sant Jordi which is indistinguishable from any other arena.

articles.title: For a Real Taste of Madrid, Skip the Michelin Meals. It’s All About the Markets.
articles.byline: Andrew Altschul and Emilio Parra Doiztua
articles.summary: Follow the locals to the city’s mercados, which offer culinary delights, flamenco classes and buzzy bars, all with a side of authenticity. Here are six hot spots.

articles.title: Alphabet’s Waymo Pulls Robotaxis Off Freeways After California Ban
articles.summary: Waymo has temporarily restricted freeway operations in the U.S., following a California ban after a few incidents involving its robotaxis.

comments.name: Michael Crawford
comments.body: I would think highway driving would be the easiest for driverless cars.  City streets have numerous variations that are hard to predict.  On a highway, it would seem sensible and relatively inexpensive to make a deal with regulators to install devices along the freeway at intervals to provide special warnings and aids and directions to the driving system, rather than depend exclusively upon onboard cameras or radars. It seems most impossible to anticipate every situation, so things that could be updated in real-time is a option.

comments.name: C Cook
comments.body:
'Fake it till you make it' was a fun objective when creating video games or assembling PCs, 

Not so good when you are pushing self driving cars,. Or, as we saw with Theranos, doing medical testing.

Too bad those funding the products are not realizing the difference.  Google execs seem to not.

comments.name: George Modica
comments.body: Imagine if California banned all motorists who are more dangerous than a Waymo!

comments.name: Scooter McGee
comments.body: Can we next focus on them:  Stopping anywhere they want including red curbs on a busy city street, going backwards out of a building entrance into oncoming traffic, running red lights (how the !@#$ did they learn that trick?!), stopping in the middle of the road blocking traffic both ways while they wait for their fare, and the other myriad of issues these garbage bins bring?

comments.name: Rick C
comments.body: So what happens when the self-drivers get hacked and told to drive too fast, run lights, etc?  Mayhem on wheels.

comments.name: Herb Idibal
comments.body: If Waymo can't do highways properly, Tesla can't even do backroads. Why in the world does Tesla think they can get away with no Lidar and radar?

comments.name: The Franks
comments.body:
Pattinson is one of the finest actors in contemporary cinema. I am utterly excited to see how he reinvents himself to fit the Bond-Genre as opposed to a Bond-Cast/Mold which is what some people are holding on to.While we have our favorite Bonds, a large part of the thrill is to see how each actor interprets a set of characteristics. 

There is no James Bond, only the actor makes him so.

comments.name: Magpie
comments.body: He is handsome, intelligent, irreverent, humorous in real life & British--could be a great fit.

comments.name: DavidHenry
comments.body: All the Bonds except Sean Connery are forgettable. Even well-intended Moore played the part like a cartoon.

comments.name: PA Observer
comments.body: I'm sure Pattinson will fit nicely in the mold of the typical James Bond we've experienced over the years. Snooze. I thought Daniel Craig was a nice departure, but now we're back to more of the old school look of the character. I'd like to be pleasantly surprised by Pattinson of course. If we're going to focus primarily on how the character should look, why not go for a striking Idris Elba sort or a suave actor like Chiwetel Ejiofor? I'm rather tired of the pale Englishmen we've been watching in that role for the last 60+ years.

comments.name: anonymouse
comments.body:
Bond is a throwback mentality being promoted as a franchise. Pattinson was cast because he's the most recognizable name of all the contenders and he shores up the franchises' weakness among female moviegoers to make it a true four quadrant franchise. Pattinson still has a lot of fans from his old days as a sparkly vampire.

No doubt the toxic masculinity aspect of Bond will be downplayed but here's the problem. Toxic masculinity IS the franchise. Without that, what is Bond? Some idiot who runs around shooting a gun wearing a tux.

comments.name: WelcomeMatt
comments.body: In my high school days, Bond novels were paperbacks and I eagerly awaited each one despite the fact that they were usually published a year apart. The first one was 1953 and it wasn't until 1962 that the first movie came out. I enjoyed all the movie versions but was shocked (a la Capt. Renault in Casablanca) when Bond ordered a Heineken)

comments.name: Farid
comments.body: Brand placements do not concern just clothes, cars, or watches. The film character himself is an ideological brand placement.

comments.name: Susan Lewis
comments.body: Oh come on stop trying to squeeze the tube. Few people in the younger generations could give a hoot about Bond. This new film is an old idea in its death throes.

articles.title: New James Bond, New James Bond Style?
articles.summary: As the Robert Pattinson era begins, many of the defining Bond brands may be about to change.

comments.name: Jerry
comments.body: I had to use the Halle airport about ten years ago. Security consisted of an imposing Frau giving Stasi-like pat-downs to each traveller. Security lines were horrendous. Who knows what else had not changed since DDR times. Perhaps this airport has been singled out for not being on par with Western German ones, and hence more vulnerable.

comments.name: Tom King
comments.body: So many sensible and sensitive comments from NYT readers from Europe, living as they do in the shadow of Russian interference; what a contrast to that American buffoon cozying up to his “friends” despite the electoral defeat he and his regime have incurred.

comments.name: Dan
comments.body:
Let me take the opportunity to report that no one in my social bubble here in Germany is convinced that Russia hires amateurs to carry out constantly failing attacks on the German infrastructure. We would expect that the Putin executive could be very successful at hitting us hard on a sub-war level any time if they only wanted to. We are waiting for proof, but there is nothing but hearsay in the media so far. 
What we do know, is that Ukrainian agents destroyed a submarine pipeline owned by the Germans at the beginning of the conflict. 
No one here feels threatended by either side, but we wish international diplomacy to get their act together asap and end this war. Thank you.

comments.name: Harry Haff
comments.body: Interesting that this stuff is happening in an area of Germany that was not very happy about reunification to begin with,

comments.name: Jim
comments.body: Are the Antonovs Russian or Ukrainian? They are described as Russian in the photo but Ukrainian Antonovs are mentioned in the article. Antonov is a Ukrainian company but made aircraft for the USSR so Russia likely still has many of their aircraft.

comments.name: Malcolm
comments.body: The Russian strategy of eroding the security of its neighbors with low-grade sabotage and mayhem is consistent with Putin’s behavior for the past 50 years.

comments.name: Perpetual Novice
comments.body:
What a great opening line --
"For years, Helmut Rost rode his bike to the edge of the Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany to pick dandelions for his rabbits."

comments.name: James
comments.body: While Putin is at war with most of the free world, Trump is in China bowing and scraping to him and Xi. This is just another sign that we have become another authoritarian nations endangering our way of life.

articles.title: These Villagers Wonder if They’re on the Front Line of Russia’s Shadow War
articles.summary: Russia is accused of clandestine attacks on Ukraine’s allies in Europe, most notably at Leipzig/Halle airport in eastern Germany. That has changed life for villagers nearby.

comments.name: Stephen Holland
comments.body: Paul's work takes me back to my salad days studying at SFSU, performing in North Beach, living my dream.  So glad to have him still with us.

comments.name: DE
comments.body:
As an SF resident it’s great to get to hear about SF’s rich artistic heritage. I wish all the best to Mr. Madonna!

That said, I think there’s a secondary item here worth a deeper look: SFMTA’s resistance to proven measures that lower the danger of our roadways. For years the city has dragged its feet on road calming measures. Safer streets that accommodate our pedestrians, cyclists, drivers, and transit users should be our goal and yet there seems to be no push coming from our mayor’s office for these reforms that he ran on. 

To the SF reporters I’d say these failures are worth a story. How is city hall failing our residents who don’t have (or can’t use) cars? How much of SF’s culture has been lost due to car-based sprawl and the resulting high infrastructure costs? How do slow infrastructure projects lead to higher costs and more dangerous streets? How can SF learn from NYC in building a city hall that works for everyone?

Thanks again to the SF reporters for both this and all the other recent SF stories!

comments.name: Lisa
comments.body:
It's obviously a miracle, that he's recovered, and to such a degree that he can apparently once again create amazing works of art.

However, what this story also once again 'drives home', so to speak, is just how positively dangerous it is, simply being inside a moving vehicle.  And yet, many drivers take that very dangerous act far, far too lightly.  Heck, people seem to exercise more care, in the privacy of their own homes, using various machinery, than they do, barreling a massive 2-Ton machine through our public space, and in such proximity to others.

I really wish this country had stricter rules about not only getting a driver's license, but the ability to maintain one.  We seem to trivialize - and have accepted - a certain level of severe injuries and deaths on our roads as simply the price that the rest of us all have to pay.  Meanwhile, the occasional 'crimes' are what typically make the headlines, with crimes committed while at the wheel, put in their own separate category (i.e., not counted as crimes).

comments.name: Miss Muffet
comments.body:
"Mr. Madonna said that he has appeared in court 29 times since the crash, but no trial date has yet been set. Mr. Giron is due back in court on Friday."

No wonder the courts are overburdened. This one should be a slam dunk.

And unacceptably stressful for the person who nearly died.

comments.name: Karen
comments.body: Paul Madonna is a local and international treasure — in addition to his extensive body of artwork which is compelling and inventive,  he is an engaging and fascinating speaker and has been featured at the Lafayette Library as well as San Francisco’s library.  I’m so grateful to hear of his latest exhibit and to know he is still pursuing his art.  We are all better for it.  His quote ‘in hard times beauty can seem frivolous, but without it all you have are hard times” has stayed with me for years and I think of it now as Paul keeps creating beauty in hard times.

comments.name: rimabird
comments.body: A longtime fan of Mr. Madonna, I have saved some of the clippings, I somehow missed the horror story of the accident and so glad to hear of his recovery.  As I, myself, have mobility issues, I won't be able to attend the gallery, but will look for his book.  Best wishes to him for a continued recovery.

comments.name: Lucy Stall
comments.body:
I salute you, Mr. Madonna, and perceive your renewed life as a miracle.  You make gorgeous work, and you’ve faced many battles.  

I wish you grace, as you continue to progress.

comments.name: Kim C
comments.body: So happy to see the Times take notice of Paul Madonna, his wonderful work, and his latest chapter. I enjoyed his column in the Chronicle for years when I first moved to San Francisco and eventually bought his book. I'm so happy to read of his recovery and continue to be utterly inspired by his work, his story, and now his resilience too.

articles.title: His Body Was Crushed in a Car Accident. His Artistry Brought Him Back.
articles.summary: Paul Madonna, known for his drawings of San Francisco landmarks, has recovered enough to have his own art exhibition four years after nearly dying in a head-on collision.

comments.name: Robert
comments.body: Was every bit as memorable as the review although set  at some times hard to connect to story. Still the bleak expressionist feeling absolutely works

comments.name: John
comments.body: I applaud a review that focuses on what matters: the singers, conductor, and the orchestra.  Productions are always tertiary. Having seen this production in Chicago years ago with Stemme and Davidson, I disagree with the positive spin here, but that doesn't matter.  Opera is singing and music.

comments.name: Andrew
comments.body: More and more performers are singing without live accompaniment - nice the see the Metropolitan Opera evolving with the times.

comments.name: Jeffrey Irving
comments.body: While I applaud your review that is more thoughtful and in depth than most of its kind these days, I find it surprising, and irresponsible as a music critic, that you made no mention of the orchestra or the conductor leading it.  Maestro Tomáš Hanus provided the deepest passion for, and understanding of, this piece … And the Met Orchestra – as well as the brilliant cast! –  responded in kind with the sort of focused and chiseled performance that this difficult music requires.  While singers are paramount in grand opera, none of it happens without an orchestra or conductor.  And a bad version of either make any great singer’s performance a miserable one!

comments.name: Squillo
comments.body: Excellent review!  Was there an orchestra in it?

comments.name: Amy
comments.body: I wish they had chosen this opera for the HD broadcast series.

comments.name: Rebes
comments.body: Amazing performance in all respects.  But why, why, is it necessary to have two 30 minute intermissions for an opera that lasts about 2 hours.  If the Met is wondering why audiences are shrinking, this is one more reason.  Coming home close to midnight on a weekday for 2 hours of (admittedly gripping) music is a big stumbling block for many

articles.title: Review: A Fearless, Ferocious New ‘Jenufa’ at the Met Opera
articles.summary: The soprano Asmik Grigorian and the tenor Sean Panikkar anchor a production by Claus Guth that allows room for its stars’ thrilling performances.

comments.name: Timothy Gill
comments.body: It would be nice if there were a map and some explanation on why they're digging in North Bergen and going east into Weehawken before it goes under the river, and showing how far it is from the current Lincoln and Holland tunnell, and what street in Manhattan it will exit at.   Also, how will the new tunnel location change NJ Transit routes?

comments.name: Riley Branch
comments.body: And those are OUR boring machines.  Musk to the rescue once again.

comments.name: Reginald V. Wedge
comments.body: Whenever the first train rolls through, Trump should be tied to the tracks.  I am not a fan of Schumer, but the Senator and fellow citizens and taxpayers deserve this win.

comments.name: Avenue Be
comments.body: And never forget Gov. Chris "time for some traffic problems in Hoboken" Christie, whose petty political ambitions delayed this project for years. Thanks Chris!

comments.name: Sharkbetty Crips
comments.body: Does the NYT need a cartographer because I’d love to apply! This is the 4th really great article Ive read today that lacked a map. In our world of decreasing geographic knowledge I believe every geographic article deserves a map.

comments.name: Stephen B
comments.body:
Hey! Those machines don't sound boring at all!

Ohhh...

comments.name: JG
comments.body: Over 120 years ago the original tunnels took 4 years to dig, passenger service began after 6 years.  One would think that our technology has advanced to the point where we'd be able to complete this faster.

comments.name: Eric
comments.body: Thank God our local governments are prevailing over the anti-infrastructure president.

articles.title: Foot by Rocky Foot, New Hudson River Rail Tunnel Begins to Take Shape
articles.summary: As the long-awaited Gateway project proceeds, two boring machines have begun digging side-by-side through some of the earth’s hardest rock.

comments.name: Rodrick Wallace
comments.body: Neither the daughter nor the son-in-law can completely prevent the grandparents from interacting with the children. There are laws about grandparents' rights. So the letter writer should tell what she has observed if she ends up giving testimony.

comments.name: Simone
comments.body:
I think they are confusing sole custody with full custody. My ex was a bully and a bulldozer when it came to getting his way. I went for and received sole custody, which worked the same as joint custody only i had the final say if there was a dispute. In 18 years I only needed to use it once. And the kids grew up knowing and spending time with both their parents. 
Any family lawyers reading this and can weigh in on the difference between those two terms?

comments.name: Mom
comments.body:
Mom of three young kids here. LW, you 100% do not have enough information to judge who is the better parent. Full stop. So much work involved in parenthood is invisible, as you might recall. Who plans and executes the birthday parties? Who gets stuff in order for the holidays? The decorations? The gifts? Who finds the pediatrician and dentist? Who schedules the appointments? Who signs the kids up for the extracurriculars? Who keeps track of deadlines for summer camp? Who responds to emails from teachers? Who buys clothes and shoes for every season? Who puts everything in the family calendar?! The list is endless. All of this is invisible, time consuming, and no fun.  

My husband travels for work. Does that mean I’m the better parent because I’m around more? No. Does anyone question his commitment to parenting? Absolutely not. Do people ask me who is taking care of my kids when I travel for work? Yes they do. 

What’s your daughter going to do about the job right now? Look for a new job during a very challenging divorce in an unpredictable economy where the threat of AI looms large? That sounds like a recipe for a mental breakdown. 

The best thing you can do is be a compassionate source of support. No judgement. Listen. Show up. Lend a helping hand. Give her a hug. When a mom feels supported, loved, understood, and valued, she is in the best position to make good life decisions.

comments.name: Mojo
comments.body: My parents divorced when I was young. Thankfully, it was a largely amicable split and custody was shared right down the middle throughout my childhood. I would say that today my parents are close friends. My mother always earned more than my father and worked a nontraditional schedule that required commuting. My father worked nights when I was a toddler to help manage childcare needs for the family. My mom was certainly always more career-minded and traditionally ambitious than my dad. However, none of these factors played any role in either's ability to parent well. For them, my needs always came first, and they did a good job ascertaining what those needs actually were. The LW doesn't seem to have a strong sense of what her grandkids need from this situation. If asked to give testimony, I would agree and stick to what the LW seems to actually know--both parents seem competent and loving, if different (which might help explain the divorce). Save your frustrations about your daughter's work life balance for a situation where they are actually relevant--such as when discussing your own relationship with her.

comments.name: SeaAlTell
comments.body:
I'm glad that the LW is thinking about what it means to be a good parent. I suggest though that they apply that focus to their own role as a parent, rather than their daughter's. 

The LW doesn't describe their daughter as perpetrating abuse. They say that she focused on her work when they were present, but perhaps she did that because they were present to help. 

Instead of thinking about testifying against their own child and instead of assuming they know what is best, perhaps they could focus on how to support their child and grandchildren. How might they demonstrate their love and caring? 

And yes, they will destroy their relationship with their daughter if they speak out against her in court without any evidence of abuse or harm.

comments.name: Nicco d'Breve
comments.body: Unless the other person is abusive or very negligent, the parent who seeks sole custody is an extremely selfish person, caring more about winning that what's best for the children. Given this, notwithstanding your perceptions and your praise, neither dad nor mom should benefit from your assistance. Hopefully the judge will be able to discern who of the two is least a narcissist, least a danger to the children's mental/psychological well-being.

comments.name: TAS
comments.body: Wow.  First time commenting on The Ethicist's responses, but I strongly disagree with this one.  The letter writer does not report ANY abuse or mistreatment of the grandkids, and may have some bias (unconscious, perhaps) against mothers, including their own daughter, who focus on their jobs. That doesn't make the daughter a "bad" parent.  It is pretty bizarre to imagine they will be testifying in court on who is the "better" parent, that sounds like a weird daydream based on some issues the grandparent has.  That  isn't going to happen, the court isn't going to let a grandparent be an arbiter of this sort of thing, but if it did why on earth would you throw your own kid under the bus when there is no evidence of abuse or mistreatment of the grandkids?  That's horrible and says something about the letter writer as a parent.  A discussion with both parents about how important it is to set aside their differences and recognize that having both parents in their lives is good for their kids is maybe in order, otherwise just focus on being a good grandparent.

comments.name: MaisyL
comments.body: This is such a naive take on how divorce and custody decisions work, both by the letter writer and by the Ethicist. Unless the children are being openly and obviously abused or neglected, it is highly unlikely either parent will receive sole custody and highly unlikely the lawyers will allow them to get to court on this issue. Certainly no court cares what the grandparents think about the mom's long work hours! Further, how any parent could even consider advocating for their adult child to have less parenting time just because the adult child is a woman who chose a demanding career (god forbid!) that funds the family lifestyle  -- including the dad's ability to be home more! - is beyond me. Maybe instead of writing to the Ethicist to ruminate on fantasy scenarios of his or her centrality, the letter writer should consider asking his or her daughter if she is doing ok and if she could use some help during this very stressful time.

articles.title: Should I Tell a Judge That My Son-in-Law Is a Better Parent Than My Daughter?
articles.summary: I strongly believe that, in the children’s best interests, the parents should share custody equally.

comments.name: Sconseter
comments.body:
Well, with the revelation that Lutnick's (sons') firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, has many investments in those same Southeast Asia computing companies as received the Nvidia chips it would seem this should have happened a lot sooner.

But no--just another example of Trump administration grift.

comments.name: Phil
comments.body:
this under the table self-dealing orchestrated by the same person who was so disgusted with Jeffrey Epstein that he told his wife we will never meet with that man again....until the family outing to Epstein's island.

Lutnick has buttered his own bread since day one of joining Trump's cabinet and could care less of US security. He needs to be let go immediately.

articles.title: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
articles.summary: The announcement appeared to be a response to recent criticism that the Commerce Department has moved too slowly on the alleged chip smuggling case.

comments.name: Kimi K
comments.body: Oh my goodness, I just retired a month ago after spending the last 7 years as a traveling healthcare provider mostly in the Riverside/San Bernardino counties and driving home to SD every weekend.  I never realized there was a Dinosaur sculpture garden in Borrego Springs. This has definitely given us a few ideas for a local trip.

comments.name: Mo
comments.body: I spent a day at Murrietta.  It was glorious.

comments.name: Sue
comments.body: I spent many happy times camping at Aqua Caliente. In the old days there was an undeveloped pool up the hill where we kids played while our parents soaked in the pool. That area is full of history - it’s part of the old stagecoach route and I remember an old mission church from the 1800’s in the little town of Pala, although I hear there is a casino there. Also near Julian is Cuyamaca state park. You can hike Stonewall peak and see into Mexico. I hope it doesn’t get all developed.

comments.name: A Dewalt
comments.body: Well written, really brings you to the place.  Also, it is what makes California so incredible.   So much to do, so beautiful.  It is worth cost of admission.  Thank you.

comments.name: Kimberley M.
comments.body: Having recently retired to upstate NY after 40 years in Southern California, this was a sweet saunter down memory lane. I would add the drive up to Idyllwild from the desert area via the 74, which takes you through the beautiful Garner Valley area, or take the tram ride up from Palm Springs. Julian in San Diego County is a charming mountain community, so I'm glad to see it was part of this trip.

comments.name: S
comments.body: Great stuff. I'm familiar with the general area but love the granularity here.

comments.name: gs
comments.body: Throw in 29 Palms and Joshua Tree Park for the art and prehistoric Native American petroglyphs. And if you drive further south along the old road along the Colorado River there are rare geoglyphs too, observable from small towers and marked by state roadside signs. Only discovered in the 1920s from the air.

comments.name: MMD
comments.body: Ooh.  Can’t wait to replicate this tour. Lived in LA most of my adult life but never been to these places. Thanks!

articles.title: Getting Into Hot Water on a Southern California Road Trip
articles.summary: Hot springs, outsider art and desert landscapes were the highlights of a four-day drive from Los Angeles to a Mexican border town and back.

comments.name: Carl
comments.body:
The Board members must be aware of their own legal liability over what has happened, even if they had no knowledge of it until recently.  To protect themselves, they will not reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. 

Good.  No CEO is indispensable.  Not Steve Jobs, not Bill Gates, certainly not Jensen Huang.

comments.name: OffToMarsForGood
comments.body: A company that respects core values won't bring back Jensen Huang. Remember, employees are watching.

comments.name: Captain Nemo
comments.location: On the Nautilus, Gulf of Texas
comments.body:
I have no doubt that Ms. Kress is supremely qualified to serve as CEO.  As its CFO perhaps even more so than Jensen Huang.  

But there is more than qualifications to fill that role.  And the biggest one is charisma.  Jensen Huang has that in spades and his charisma is inseparably bound to NVIDIA.  Ms. Kress simply doesn’t have the performative skills to appropriate and exceed Huang’s that in the eyes of the investors.  The drop in share value despite outstanding enumerators clearly shows that.  With a doubling of revenue within a single quarter, the shares should have more than recovered their losses.  That they went up only a measly 2% underscores my point.

Bring Huang back ASAP!

comments.name: Not A Seer
comments.body: Employees don’t get it. Their leader broke the rules, and there will be consequences—for the company as well as him personally. He’s made their jobs harder. And who knows what other bad behavior will come out of the investigations. There is no going back.

comments.name: Balanced Noise
comments.body: The head of the Nvidia dragon has just been severed. Collette has a challenging job to steady or change the body.  60 direct reports sounds like a confucian culture. Some employees may have been touched at an "emotional level".  However, it sounds to me that fear was a bigger factor, with Jensen's daughter being the senior enforcer on the Confucian org chart.  I imagine many of the 60 direct reports were Jensen's sychophants, spies, or chronies who will be in job preservation mode, and their number one goal will to undermine Collette to ensure another of their club is installed as CEO to preserve their role and power.  From what I'm reading, I'm sure she sees it and will do what's necessary to guide Nvidia appropriately in the interim.  To do so, more than the head of the dragon will need to go!

comments.name: Jesse Lee
comments.body: The term ‘not ready for prime time’ comes to mind.

comments.name: Andrew Stevens.
comments.body: Good to see they still plan to sell to any buyer and help play both sides of the water.

comments.name: Paulette Altmaier
comments.body: No CFO is going to get the trust or respect from employees to lead a tech company.  Nor should they.

articles.title: Nvidia’s Interim C.E.O. Tries to Soothe a Rattled Company: ‘We’ve Got This.’
articles.summary: At an all-hands meeting with employees, Colette Kress sought to put the indiscretions of Nvidia’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, behind them.

comments.name: California expat
comments.body: A handful of obscenely greedy people should not be in charge of the future of humanity.

comments.name: Tristan
comments.body: Well? Where’s the cure for just one type of cancer, or any inroad in climate change? Just a morsel of meaningful progress in these two headline promises would make public opinion far less averse to handing vast money and power to these folks.

comments.name: Midfleclassmanifesto
comments.body:
existential risks to the digital world for sure

for the World as a whole a Big Chance

to go back to Analogic

it was a wild ride from Big Tech to Back to Analogue

very fast, big money for very few , good fun for many

the really bad part was the damage to language , schools, minds. 

but Humanity has seen and sees worse

comments.name: gs
comments.body:
For all its impressive power, AI will not repeal the laws of physics and biology. It is contributing to global warming, with its insatiable hunger for electricity, faster than it is finding a solution to it.
And while a cure for cancer may be a utopian dream, the solution for global warming is already known: convert to existing renewable energy sources and stop eating beef.
Meanwhile, AI is quite impressive in drafting lawyer’s letters and analyzing medical reports. But does that justify covering the planet in rapacious data centers?

comments.name: Felix
comments.body:
Vague promises like "curing cancer" are no justification for running unpredictable experiments on society to serve investors' interests.

This is why we need true alternatives like a cosy AI. The NYT covers big tech and venture capital driven AI labs like Anthropic, but gives little attention to initiatives that actually want to do something about this insanity.

comments.name: Jbjab
comments.body: All the things AI “can” help with, like curing diseases, don’t seem to be in the works. Instead, it’s all about hyper-charging google searches. Unimaginable wealth has clouded the humanity of our tech (soon to be) overlords.

comments.name: Sigurd
comments.body:
The only ones who pose existential risk to humanity are we, the humans. Despite warnings for hundreds of years  we don’t care, destroying out environment, ourselves and dozens of other species without remorse. 
So this will be hard to beat by AI.

comments.name: pacovar
comments.body: "If" the pivot on which the future unfolds. Given our capacity as humans it seems likely the balance will fall predominantly towards the dark rather than the light.

articles.title: Big Money, Existential Risks
articles.summary: Anthropic’s prospectus for its blockbuster I.P.O. this week reads like dystopian science fiction.

comments.name: henri cervantes
comments.body: Coca is not cocaine. Just sayin’.

comments.name: Mak
comments.body: Really,how much could a babysitter cost back then?

comments.name: CB
comments.body: Cocaine is a modern invention.  It was invented by the Germans.  The children were most likely ingesting some sort of product made from coca leaves, or the leaves themselves.  But it was not cocaine.

comments.name: LuluNYC
comments.body: Do researchers know how the children were actually killed? The whole notion is just so horrifying to our modern Western sensibilities. I find it impossible to imagine these children welcomed this role foisted upon them. Probably any reticence is why they were drugged.

comments.name: Paul
comments.body: I recently visited the museum in Argentina where these mummified children are being studied. Remarkably the children show no sign at all of fear or distress— they just look like sleeping children. As hideous as the practice is to us, the Incas saw things very differently. To appease or thank their gods, they sacrificed what was most precious to them.

comments.name: sphilipr
comments.body: I've been listening to 'The Rest is History' podcast who remark that the Romans were horrified that the Ancient Britons practised human sacrifice whilst (they wryly point out) seeing no problem at all with sending home slaves to be killed in the coliseum for public amusement. Modern American observers might look in horror at Incan child sacrifice whilst seeing similarly no problem with the ownership of guns that have twice resulted in the multiple deaths of similar aged children in American schools. In both cases it's what passes for morality.

comments.name: MT
comments.body: Anybody who has walked the Inca trail has had the experience of being offered coca leaves to help with the altitude sickness, even today. It has trace amounts of cocaine. Perhaps a more accurate picture than kids being forced to do lines of coke as suggested by the article.

comments.name: Sylvia
comments.body:
As cruel as the sacrificing and the giving of drugs beforehand was, it was part of the Inca culture, founded in their world and seen as promising. We shouldn't forget that at the same time, in what was relatively enlightened Europe, thousands of people, especially women, were burned as witches. Without having received any drugs beforehand. 

And by the way, there was no cocaine in Inca times. Chewing coca leaves can't be compared to the effect of cocaine.

articles.title: Inca Children Were Given Cocaine and Ayahuasca Before Being Sacrificed
articles.summary: A toxicological study of frozen mummies from the Andes sheds light on what happened before a sacred ritual of the Inca Empire.

comments.name: Gia
comments.body: The LOTR trilogy is my all-time favorite; they even inspired me to read the books, which I couldn't be bothered with as a kid when all my friends were reading them. My husband and I tried to get into the Rings of Power, but one episode into season three, and we tapped out. It was beginning to spoil the whole franchise for me, so I decided to stick with what I love and watch the movies.

comments.name: Tim Cali
comments.body:
The great triumph of Peter Jacksons production is that when people with commitment and vision (Jackson & Boykins) proposed it to a studio where the decision makers (story tellers seem to have made the decision) embraced that vision and empowered Jackson et al to expand to 3 films.  This was in a modern age a truly rare combination of vision empowered by freedom from the bean counters.
ROP by contrast is a small, myopic bean counters exploit to try to increase the dragon's hoard (what are another few gold coins worth under the mountain), and which is run by show runners that are either hobbled by the bean counters, or are unworthy of anything beyond a weekly sitcom.

comments.name: Ad absurdum per aspera
comments.body:
> “The Shadow that bred them can only mock, it cannot make: not real new things of its own.”

A thought worth keeping in mind as, Eru help us,  we enter the age of AI slop...

comments.name: Guy
comments.body: I miss poor, doomed Celebrimbor, who made the second season watchable.

comments.name: Joel Fritz
comments.body: I'm not as displeased as the author, but agree that the series could be better.  I know that the story is based on the appendix to the LOTR trilogy which I enjoyed reading 60 years ago.  It's a dry chronicle, something an academic like Tolkien knew how to write.  It could have been fleshed out better.  The major characters have some banal traits that are contrary to the epic orientation of the Tolkien stories.  I'm also not happy with the amount of hand to hand combat that includes both gross amounts of splatter and highly choreographed fencing.  The characters dance through battles lopping of limbs as they go.  I expect them to break into song.

comments.name: Macaulay
comments.body: Tolkien was an arch-reactionary who described The Lord of the Rings as "a fundamentally religious and Catholic work," loathed automobiles and the liturgical reforms of Vatican II, and was more at home in the world of Beowulf, the Eddas, and Northern mythology than in the 20th century.   That is why The Lord of the Rings is so good and so popular - no one else wrote like him.  Modernist-minded critics generally have little appreciation for Tolkien, e.g. Edmund Wilson, who wrote that "Dr. Tolkien has little skill at narrative and no instinct for literary form."   It would take a select group to do Tolkien well - his fans were fortunate with Peter Jackson.  Guess lightning doesn't strike twice!

comments.name: Al Orin
comments.body:
Was looking forward to Season One but couldn't get past the first few episodes. How could Tolkien's majestic and complex works be translated into such dull, prosaic, cliched television? The characters were flat and actually characterless, when they were not simply wrongheaded and offensive. Galadriel as petulant and pouty? Really?

The books convey elves and elvish society as enlightened and magical but the elves we meet on TV are just banal humans with pointy ears and their society is quite mundane. The same goes to a lesser extent for the Numenoreans, who live for hundreds of years under elvish guidance - and yet end up, on TV, as prosaic and uninteresting.

As the article points out, once any of these TV series leave the magisterial source material, Hollywood is unable to generate the interesting, complex, magical dialogue and stories that made the original novels so compelling. Just look at every time Peter Jackson's crew thought they were being clever and diverged from Tolkien's storyline - the results ranged from lamentable to laughable.

comments.name: TM
comments.body: I do love to disagree with Mr Poniewozik but I’m afraid I have to agree with him this time. A fix to this series, and oh so many others, would be to add a few more writers to the team. Maybe some who specialize in dialogue. I’m really trying not to be snarky here but the acting talent is strong enough, the show looks great for the most part, it just needs to be more compelling.

articles.title: In ‘The Rings of Power,’ I.P.-Based TV Loses Its Magic
articles.summary: The costly Tolkien extravaganza, now in its third season, is a monument to the scale and forgettability of many of TV’s franchise spinoffs.

comments.name: Nathalee
comments.body:
Personally, I would not choose to become an influencer because I am aware of how toxic people in social media are. It is toxic to the point that when you are known, just one flaw about you would almost, if not fully, end your “career” and get you in to cancel culture. Though if i were to become an influence, i would most probably create silent, calm, and relaxing “A day in my life” videos. Just quietly sharing how my day goes without a word because in today’s time, one wrong word that you say will stick in people's minds and that will immediately “help” them conclude what type of person you are even without knowing you personally, and the hate that you will receive can go above and beyond. 

At the end of the day, nobody is perfect and every individual makes or will make mistakes. A person's worth should never be defined by a single flaw, mistake, or opinions of others.

comments.name: Brighton Norton
comments.body: If I was an influencer I would probably post things like the constant crafts and ideas I come up with that other people might like to use as inspiration too. I love making and doing things by hand. I love the process of trial and error. I love to make new things that I can benefit from. I think that I would be a good influencer because people could find me as someone safe to support. And I want to encourage other people to express themselves safely. I also would hope people find comfort in me and the things I do and become comfortable. The world can feel unsafe to people right now with everything that's happening and I want to provide a moment of relaxation for the people in worry and help them feel safe.

comments.name: Reagan Westfield
comments.body: Content creation seems fun, it also seems like a big dedication. Personally I would never choose it over a steady 9-5, it kind of depends on the job but the job I want right now is way better than influencing. In the article it states how she gets brand deals and all of  that cool stuff but to be honest I would rather have a steady job. Content creation just isn't what interests me as of right now.

comments.name: Cataleya Walden
comments.body:
Honestly, the concept of being an influencer sounds interesting, and even quite fun, but at the same time, it seems like it takes serious determination and dedication, and can often look quite tiresome. I mean, sure, it looks like it’ll be fun being able to tell your fans what you eat or do in a day. But at the same time, being an influencer comes with you being on thin ice all of the time. Do or say the wrong thing, and next thing you know…you’re cancelled. Or, don’t fit the standards and stereotypes that everyone has set for influencers, and no one will engage with your content. 

And, if I’m being honest, the statistics of most people picking an influencer job over a regular 9-to-5 isn’t all too surprising. From their perspective, sure, it may seem appalling for those to create some false internet persona that everyone bases their life on, but from my perspective, I’d rather have a job that relies on me using my actual, useful life skills and knowledge, and would prioritize my safety and comfort over the satisfaction of strangers on the internet.

comments.name: Corinne Gazda
comments.body: For me, this article did not change my opinions of life as an influencer. Since creating content is what gets them paid, I feel regular content and constant recording is not an extreme task. However, this life can be hard with many downsides. It would be hard to take a break and be alone, and I would imagine it can disrupt your relationships. In addition, influencers can receive hate but are at the same time pressured to not take time for themselves. This can be hard, and it would not be the life I would want, but this is the life Haley chose, and it is the job she wanted. Besides the downsides, being an influencer does have its appeal. Getting free merch and money would be nice, considering you can get it just from doing what you love. It could also lead to more fame, so you could transition more into what you are making content about. For example, say the downsides became too much for Ms. DeKreek, she could still use her platform to become a marketer or modeler. I think being an influencer who was always online would not be healthy for me or anyone, but could bring great opportunities that eventually make it worth it.

comments.name: Gianfranco Montalto
comments.body: The recent survey in the article stating 4 in 10 gen Z respondents would take a social media job instead of a 9 to 5 job does make sense to me as I also would like to be a gaming influencer at some point (even though I never get around to recording a video even when I have the software). I would like to be on because it seems fun to make money off of playing different games as I like playing many different types of videogames and could have fun white making money. While a 9 to 5 job seems like it has stable pay unlike being an influencer which could change its income at random. Also you would have to be recording a lot of your time or you will make less videos which causes people to stop watching your videos. While it would be fun I feel like being online and recording that much makes it less worth it but I could see myself doing that like once a week. Then you have the issue of having to edit your videos causing it to take even longer to get a video out. In conclusion I wouldn't take it over a 9 to 5 job although I might still do it a bit in my free time.

comments.name: Jonah S.
comments.body: My reaction is honestly not surprising. I know that some influencers are how they act on camera, but some people fake their entire persona online. I also know how brand deals obviously sponsor influencers a ton. Some people don’t take brand deals even though they are offered some. It makes a lot of sense, because I just assumed it would be how Ms. DeKreek’s life is, and from my understanding, I am correct. Influencers almost always hide how they actually are online. The main reason they do this is for engagement bait. This is when they either be controversial, or just say/do stupid things to keep viewers watching. Some influencers have the mindset of: every kind of attention is good attention. This obviously means people will get into stupid arguments just for views and clips. I thought that the video stood out to me as the one thing I didn’t realize with those kinds of influencers is how much preparation there actually is. There seemed to be a whole process of everything before Ms. DeKreek even started recording. I watch some influencers, but not influencers like her. The video gave me some insight on the preparation that occurs before a video. It also made me think about how she only has 50,000 people following her, imagine how people prepare with millions of followers. I think one of the main downsides is the pressure to make sure the videos are good, with the upside making lots of money. I’d feel uncomfortable if a camera was always on, but I’d get used to it eventually.

comments.name: Max Tyler
comments.body: Personally, my reaction is “Wow”. Before this, I basically thought that influencers just recorded videos for like an hour a day, but hearing about the “always on cam” that rocked my understanding. I follow jynxzi and Joe Bartolozzi, who both make content AND stream. I love them both because they are both funny and brighten my day. I have wondered about what life is like for them, though. Joe Bart streams about four hours a day, and jynxzi streams about 8 hours a day. Let’s take jynxzi for example. He is basically working a 9-5 where all day long he has to be funny and silly. I feel like after his streams, his life probably feels a bit burnt out. He also streams at weird hours too, though, like 7pm to 3am, so he must be relieved to sleep. I feel like once you are an influencer, it can be pretty easy if you’re at the top, but working your way up to the top must be extremely frustrating and hard.

articles.title: Would You Want to Be an Influencer?
articles.summary: Haley DeKreek, a 20-year-old junior, is part of the sorority TikTok boom, with 45,000 TikTok followers and several paid brand deals. Is that a life you would like for yourself — even if it means always having the camera on?

comments.name: Lomg Time Reader
comments.body: One of the places on the list is the Fresh Meadows residential complex in Queens, where I grew up. Fresh Meadows was built and planned as a complete community on the former Fresh Meadows Country Club and golf course. It is notable for its preservation of open spaces and its sense of scale. Unfortunately it appears to be under threat today as the current owners are seeking to add many new large structures in what for almost 80 years have been unique green spaces.  If this is permitted it will be a tremendous loss for those who live there and the City as a whole.  The City of Yes will destroy something irreplaceable.

"we have to rise above our prejudices"

When I finally began treatment a few months ago with Lexapro, an SSRI, the problem basically disappeared within a couple weeks.

comments.name: Colenso

comments.name: Westerner
comments.body: As a former ruminator myself, I think a lot of people would just rather think about it than do it. They may think there is some magic formula or secret that will make them high performing individuals. In many cases, we hide behind the absurd fiction that our effectiveness and productivity suffer because we are “perfectionists.” In reality, we are just victims of our own psychic inertia. Productivity and accomplishments depend on action. Action requires the input of energy. Stop,making excuses and just do something.

comments.name: Nora
comments.body:
I ask myself this question: Is there anything I can do about this? If there is, I do it. If there isn't, I don't spend any more time worrying, because that only makes things worse.

I used to practice what I called "prophylactic pessimism," but I stopped when I realized it was hurting more than it helped - how much time had I wasted thinking the worst when everything turned out fine? And even when everything didn't turn out fine, I was calmer before whatever it was, and better able to face it.

comments.name: Bradley
comments.body: The best example of ruminating, in simple poetry terms, is Shel Silverstein's "Whatif"poem: "Last night, while I lay thinking here, some Whatifs crawled inside my ear, and pranced and partied all night long, and sang their same old Whatif song..." His poems were read to me as a child. I've known this poem my whole life. To this day, when I catch myself ruminating, or a family member or good friend, I start to recite it out loud. Somehow it slows me down.

comments.name: Busy Bee
comments.body: When I was going through a divorce I found myself ruminating about lots of issues, finances, family, anger, the future, etc.  I found several things helped.  First, I limited where and when I could ruminate (only in the car and only in the daytime, for 5 minutes at a time).  If I found myself ruminating at another time I paused and reminded myself of my rules.  And after my 5 minutes of ruminating I would imagine that all my problems were scattered all over my attic floor, and I would in my mind start sweeping them into a pile and them push them into a hole.  The process of sweeping minimized the problems for me and allowed me to focus on what I could control.   This is a process I have used over the past 15 years and have saved me a lot of sleepness nights.

comments.name: juan swift
comments.body: It would be helpful if the reviewer, Prof. Wood, who knows a great deal about Latin American literature, would explain that the term "magical realism" was a marketing tool and an inadequate translation of "lo real maravilloso," a term coined by Alejo Carpentier, the Cuban-French novelist, in the prologue to his historical novel "The Kingdom of this World," about Haiti. Carpentier's argument was that the surrealism that European artists sought to create through aesthetics existed in the reality of daily life and ritual in the Caribbean and Latin America. García-Márquez celebrated Carpentier's insight and expanded on it, much as the Colombian painter Botero does in his Rabelaisian vision of the Colombian ruling class. Vargas-Llosa, a realist, whose literary models were Flaubert and Hugo, uses the tools of European 19th- and 20th-century prose, as Prof. Wood observes, to critique and push back against the mythical and metaphysical in 20th-century Latin America that so-called "magical realism" celebrates. Instead of folklorizing Latin America, he writes about it with a jaundiced eye, using the tools of literary modernism. (Which is why "The Feast of the Goat" and "Conversation in the Cathedral" are two of his finest works). Although he is a brilliant stylist--better, one could argue, than García-Marquez--his lack of empathy for the poor and the marginal in his works mirrors the cruelty of the politics of his  heroes Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan.

comments.name: Guillermo
comments.body: A great novelist may not necessarily aspire to perfection in his own life, rather than that, the opposite is usually closer to the norm. Vargas Llosa had a powerful narrative that made his novels unique, with an inspiration in French nineteenth century novel, but with many other influences from Spanish and Latin American literary tradition, as well as English and American literature, etc that made his stories appealing both as an entertainment as well as reflecting a deeper connection with Western cultural traditions and creating a new form of storytelling. Moving away from Marxist revolution instead of enjoying the views from a tropical garden in Havana near Castro only showed his commitment to liberal values, while his criticism to Dominican Republic dictatorship in his novel La fiesta del chivo or criticism of Fujimori when he ran against him in Peru presidential elections also show that he was against attacks to democracy that could turn into dictatorships without any label. His consciousness about the historical decadence of Latin American countries, perhaps also about its metropoli in Spain which he also loved and enjoyed and how things could have been done differently is perhaps also one of his characteristics. He may have lacked enough social consciousness in his approach to politics but at least he wrote some of the best novels ever written in Spanish and was a staunch supporter of democracy in difficult times, which outweighs any criticism towards him

comments.name: Randall
comments.body: What a strange review, or else what a very weird biography.  I would appear from what I've just read here, that either the reviewer has failed to read the full scope of Vargas Llosa Nobel prize winning life's accomplishments.  Or are they simply , both or one or the other, insensitive to the range of the author's interests, or of the influence of French literature and the history of the DeGaulle 5th Republic years on his writing and political development in the 1970s.  It seems particularly curious that either the review or the biographer found Vargas Llosa's turn away from the revolutionary left in response to the Shining Path destruction of Peruvian social and financial stability, or the corruption of the forces that brought the Japanese immigrant and later prisoner convicted not only of theft but of connivance in assassination to the Peruvian presidency.  As an admirer of Vargas Llosa's witty social commentary on romance, the Latin lover, popular entertainment on radio and television, the perils of youthful lust and geriatric priapism, rustic elopement, the terror of riding a bus into Shining Path territory, the primitive Marxism of urban guerrillas who could never decide on an action.  And then to say he wrote 4 good books, and the 3 first were his best.  I guess I'll have to wait for a real biography or a better informed reviewer.

comments.body: In addition to beautiful architecture, the North Side is notable for its many public staircases. The Rising Main St Steps are almost 400 steps tall, while others are shorter but connect to scenic spots like the Fineview Overlook. Pittsburgh has one of the highest rates of walking to work in the US, meaning many of these staircases are important transportation infrastructure and not just historic relics. Unfortunately the North Side was hit hard by highway construction in the 20th century and many former thriving neighborhoods were destroyed so commuters could drive to Butler County more quickly.

comments.body: I'm excited to see the changes since I lived there until 1990. My house was in Perry Hilltop, above the north side. My husband and I used to walk down a steep set of stairs and cross some neighborhood streets to go to Pirate games at the all-purpose stadium that existed then. Back then, the area was not exceptionally safe for walking, but we were young. Good to see that old-timers and newcomers can coexist in this redeveloped area.

I'll take Pittsburgh or Buffalo. I am a champion of legacy cities and neighborhoods. I enjoy contributing to the next chapter of their history, culture and charm.

comments.name: Jim Murray
comments.body: Glad and sad to read this.  It is architecturally a glorious place to live and was always so. Andrew Carnegie grew up here in poverty and started the free library movement there. The public parks are amazing. Build quality of the row houses is beyond solid. I remember the City selling houses there for $100 if you remodeled them. The reason was simple. Hate to say it but the inner city community moved in and white flight began. That was the deterioration start in the 1960s. Poor people just did not care what they had. The schools? I was part of the forced bussing that was a social disaster. Decent children pushed into schools with children of neglect and poverty, that reduced the education quality of the the first group but no one cared as it served a liberal social bias.  I saw more than one kid getting an object shoved into his rectum in a shower as middle school kids laughed. Teachers were no were around. It was the first time I ever saw a teacher physically attacked in a hallway.  I believe in public schools but Pittsburgh failed us and merrily goes on ignoring the criminal activity permitted on children in the name of integration. Race riots were common at Oliver High School then on the the North Side.  Best argument ever for vouchers, if you wanted an education you went to the Catholic schools for it. It's a great place now that the poverty has been pushed out. And, you know what, I'm a liberal but sometimes the price for that is paid by the others.

comments.name: Anonymous
comments.body: "Diverse"is the key,and the success of bringing back struggling areas of U.S. cities depends upon the broadest interpretation of the word:especially embracing "affectional" diversity.St. Louis,MO.,has a North Side, too.I was born there,and I spent my earliest years watching the incomprehensible flight of all my White friends.By 1964 all my White friends on Clarence Avenue were gone, and probably the only reason we weren't gone, too, is because my grandfather owned the building. Whether my friends were Black or White meant nothing to me, and I benefitted from a unique affection my African-American friends' families had for the "type" of Italian my immigrant grandfather was,a Sicilian. Later, when I taught at the Science and Math Magnet High School across the street on Clarence from where I spent my first 10 years, a girl in one of my classes said, "I wouldn't marry a White man, but I'd marry an Italian." The highest compliment I ever got and now I'm 75 with the most beautiful half-Haitian grandsons.But as much as racial intolerance (in St. Louis's case with the most brutal police oppression that finally led to Ferguson),I think it was the "affectional" intolerance,for there's a massive correlation between those cities and even towns around America that have embraced the Gay Community and enjoyed a renaissance,that destroyed it.Even here now in a backwater of intolerance, Hunterdon County,NJ,the 2 places,Lambertville and Frenchtown, with large Gay Communities that are thriving.
